gaps.summary:
For this engine, animation should mean changing parameters of the solved frame over time, not adding a separate animation layer. The engine already computes dominant curves with native arc length (clothoids, log spirals, circles) and an attachment graph, and those two things decide most of the design.

The browser facts point to three runtime tiers. (A) A rigid motif travelling along a track, like the owner's medallion "arrows", is best done as Web Animations API transform keyframes sampled from the track by arc length. Transform is on Chromium's compositor list (I read the source); offset-distance/offset-path is not. Composited means the motion keeps running while Vue renders the new section. (B) Draw-in and "ink pulse" effects use stroke-dashoffset with pathLength=1. Because the engine draws lines as filled outlines, these need mask-reveal (Colloseus' calligraphy technique). This runs on the main thread but is cheap. (C) True shape changes (a weave ripple, leaf growth) re-solve a small subgraph each frame in requestAnimationFrame.

Built-in options each have problems. CSS offset-path is Baseline but path() takes px only, url() and shape() are newer, and none of them run on the compositor in Chromium. SMIL works but CSS cannot control it. GSAP is free but under a proprietary Webflow licence. Rive and Lottie bake geometry at authoring time, and Rive exports have needed a paid plan since 20 Oct 2025. Theatre.js has not had a public release since May 2024.

For site-section changes, same-document View Transitions now work in all three engines, but they snapshot as raster, so the frame must stay out of the snapshot. Pause motion when the document is hidden and honour prefers-reduced-motion. Keep every motion event-triggered and under 5 s, which avoids the WCAG 2.2.2 pause requirement. The motion layer should stay small. SVG and Canvas perform about the same, and both slow down when roughly 8,000 elements are redrawn.

findings.item: CSS Motion Path (offset-path / offset-distance / offset-rotate): support
findings.facts: MDN calls offset-path Baseline Widely available since March 2022 and notes that some parts are supported unevenly. MDN BCD (raw JSON read 2026-10-10): offset-path Chrome 55, Firefox 72, Safari 15.4. path() Chrome 64, Firefox 72, Safari 16. url() Chrome 116, Firefox 122, Safari 17. Basic shapes and coord-box Chrome 116, Firefox 122, Safari 18. ray() Chrome 116, Firefox 122, Safari 16. Caniuse shows full support at 96.84% of global usage, and the spec is still a Working Draft. url() can reference an SVG path, circle, rect and similar shapes. In SVG the default coord-box is view-box. MDN's shape() page says path() is limited to px units.
findings.use_for_engine: Don't use offset-path:path() for page-sized tracks. Its px-only coordinates break on every resize, and the engine would have to rewrite the string. offset-path:url(#track-id), pointing at the engine's own hidden track path, is the only CSS form that should follow re-solved geometry automatically. I have not tested that it updates live when 'd' changes, so verify it in the Lab. In any case, prefer the WAAPI-transform method (see the Chromium compositor finding).

findings.item: CSS shape() function (responsive paths for clip-path and offset-path)
findings.facts: MDN marks shape() as Baseline 2026, newly available since February 2026. It is defined for border-shape, clip-path and offset-path. It accepts %, rem, em and calc(), where path() accepts px only, so shapes scale with the reference box. BCD: Chrome 135, Firefox 148, Safari 18.4. The BCD entry does not separate offset-path support from clip-path support.
findings.use_for_engine: shape() could give a responsive CSS track with no JS for simple percentage-defined curves. But the engine's curves are solved (clothoid and log-spiral fits) and can't be expressed in percentages, and the support is new. Keep it as a fallback idea only, and check offset-path: shape() in each target browser before relying on it.

findings.item: What Chromium can run on the compositor (read from current source)
findings.facts: In blink compositor_animations.cc on main (fetched 2026-10-10), the properties that can be composited are opacity, transform/translate/rotate/scale, filter and backdrop-filter. background-color, clip-path and box-shadow use paint-worklet paths, and custom properties are composited only when a paint worklet uses them. No offset-* property is listed, so offset-distance animations run on the main thread. SVG-specific rules from the same file: only the 'transform' property can be composited on SVG elements, not individual translate/rotate/scale. Elements that have SMIL animations are refused. Elements inside an SVG resource such as a mask, clipPath or pattern are refused. A transformable container with an extra transform is refused, and the code comment names '<use> x/y attributes' and <svg>/<symbol> viewBox transforms. Non-1 zoom and vector-effect also block compositing. The Chrome blog (last updated 2021-02-22) says hardware-accelerated SVG animations have been on by default since Chromium 89.
findings.use_for_engine: This changes the current code. Ornaments are placed as <use href x= y= width= height=> in src/frames/frameEngine.ts:210 and framing/render/svg.ts:38, and Chromium won't composite a transform animation on those. Put any element that moves inside a <g> with only a transform, or in a small HTML-level wrapper. Composited (Tier A) motion should animate 'transform' only. Mask-based reveals and dash animations will always run on the main thread.

findings.item: Safari/WebKit compositing of SVG child elements
findings.facts: Igalia's posts describe the Layer-Based SVG Engine (LBSE) as in WebKit but not the default (21 May 2024). A 29 June 2026 update covers making layer creation conditional and doesn't say LBSE is on by default anywhere. I found no source confirming that Safari composites transform animations on SVG child elements.
findings.use_for_engine: For a guaranteed composited traveller in every engine, render the moving glyph in its own small absolutely positioned element (an HTML wrapper holding a tiny SVG) in page coordinates, and animate its CSS transform. The static frame stays in the big SVG.

findings.item: SMIL <animateMotion>
findings.facts: MDN calls it Baseline Widely available since January 2020. It supports path, an <mpath> reference, keyPoints/keyTimes, rotate=auto|auto-reverse, and calcMode defaults to 'paced' (constant speed). Chrome's 2015 'Intent to deprecate: SMIL' was suspended in August 2016 ('we've decided to suspend our intent to deprecate and take smaller steps toward other options'). Chromium refuses to composite elements that have SMIL animations (source above). Jake Archibald's 2013 article said SMIL 'performs poorly' in Chrome and Safari.
findings.use_for_engine: Avoid SMIL for the site. CSS media queries can't control it, so reduced motion would need JS (SVGSVGElement.pauseAnimations), it blocks compositing, and its future has been uncertain since 2016. Its useful ideas are paced timing and keyPoints, and the engine gets both from its own arc-length tables.

findings.item: Web Animations API (Element.animate)
findings.facts: MDN calls it Baseline Widely available since March 2020 (BCD: Chrome 36, Firefox 48, Safari 13.1). It returns a controllable Animation (play, pause, reverse, currentTime, finished promise). It accepts timeline, rangeStart and rangeEnd for scroll or view timelines. MDN advises respecting prefers-reduced-motion.
findings.use_for_engine: Use this as the runtime for Tier A. Sample the solved track at uniform arc-length steps (for example 64 to 128 keyframes), and give each keyframe {transform: translate(x,y) rotate(θ), offset: s/L}. Put the speed profile in the effect easing. The motion is then composited, has constant speed along the curve, and can be cancelled or seeked. A resize can rebuild the keyframes and restore currentTime.

findings.item: stroke-dasharray / stroke-dashoffset line drawing and pathLength
findings.facts: Jake Archibald (2013) set the dash and gap to getTotalLength(), set the offset to the length, and transitioned stroke-dashoffset to 0. You need to force layout between setting the start and end values. MDN pathLength: the browser scales all distance calculations by pathLength divided by the computed length, so stroke-dasharray treats the path as running from 0 to pathLength. getPointAtLength is Baseline Widely available since January 2020. Polygon's PS4 and Xbox One reviews (Vox Media, 25 Nov 2013) used this technique on Illustrator-traced line art, after cleaning up Illustrator's SVG export by hand.
findings.use_for_engine: Set pathLength="1" on every animatable stroked spine. Dash values are then fractions of arc length and stay valid when the engine re-solves the curve at a new page size, so no getTotalLength call is needed after a resize. One dash window, a dash d plus a gap with an offset driven by time, gives draw-in, draw-out and a travelling 'pulse'. Dash changes repaint on the main thread.

findings.item: Mask-reveal for filled, variable-width outlines
findings.facts: In 'Animate Calligraphy with SVG' (Claus Colloseus, CSS-Tricks, 22 June 2018), a smooth path is stroked wide enough to cover the brush outline and used as a mask. The mask path's stroke-dashoffset is then animated. It has to be a mask, because clip-path ignores strokes. Where strokes overlap, the drawing is split into pieces that don't overlap, stacked in drawing order, each with its own mask, and tangents are matched at the joins. Sequencing can use CSS keyframes with holds or SMIL begin chains.
findings.use_for_engine: The engine draws lines as filled outlines with width profiles, and the weave generator already produces RibbonPiece[] split at crossings with over/under and halo. That matches the precondition here. Each piece gets a mask from its own centreline, offset by the piece's start s on the strand. The reveal then flows across crossings and is hidden correctly where the strand passes under. In Chromium, mask content is never composited.

findings.item: requestAnimationFrame with your own arc-length parameterisation
findings.facts: MDN: rAF callbacks generally run at the display refresh rate (60, 75, 120 or 144 Hz). Use the timestamp to compute progress, 'otherwise, the animation will run faster on high refresh-rate screens'. All callbacks in one frame get the same timestamp. rAF calls are paused in most browsers in background tabs and hidden iframes. Pomax's Bézier primer: t does not map linearly to distance, so build a lookup table of t to cumulative length and invert it to find the closest t for a given distance.
findings.use_for_engine: Use one MotionDirector with a single rAF loop for Tiers B and C, and compute every motion from the timestamp. The engine's analytic curves are already in arc length (a clothoid is defined by s, and log spirals and circles have closed-form s). Only fitted cubics and composite paths need a lookup table, built once per solve and never per frame.

findings.item: GSAP MotionPathPlugin and licence status
findings.facts: Licence: the 'Standard No Charge GSAP License', effective 30 April 2025 and modified 30 May 2025. All plugins are free for commercial use. It is proprietary, owned by Webflow, and not MIT. Prohibited without consent: use in 'tools that allow users to build visual animations without code' that compete with Webflow. Webflow can amend or terminate the licence. npm gsap 3.15.0 was published 2026-04-13 under that licence. MotionPathPlugin.min.js is about 22 KB minified and gsap.min.js about 73 KB (measured from unpkg). Features: path from an SVG element, data or points; align, autoRotate, start and end (which can wrap); resolution defaults to 12 for even speed. The docs say alignment is computed once at the start and is not re-measured on resize. They suggest saving progress, killing the tween, rebuilding it and jumping back to that progress.
findings.use_for_engine: It works, but it adds about 95 KB and a proprietary licence to do what the engine's arc-length sampler plus WAAPI already does. It also doesn't follow re-solved geometry. The Frame Lab is effectively a visual animation-building tool, which is close to the licence's prohibited-use wording if it were ever shared. Use the 'record progress, rebuild, seek' pattern, not the library.

findings.item: Rive (state machines, Follow Path, web runtime)
findings.facts: Runtime Sizes page (January 2026), brotli-compressed: canvas-lite 222 KB (707 KB uncompressed), canvas 567 KB, webgl2 648 KB, mostly WASM. Rendering is canvas or WebGL, not DOM SVG. Since 20 October 2025, new exports need a paid plan (Cadet: $9/month annually, $17 monthly). Runtimes remain MIT, there is no runtime fee, and existing exports keep working. Luau scripting launched 13 January 2026 with Node, Converter, Layout, Test and PathEffect protocols. The announcement doesn't say which runtimes run scripts. State machines connect timeline animations through states and transitions. Follow Path (covered in research file 05) attaches an object at a percentage distance and orients it to the tangent.
findings.use_for_engine: Its concepts are worth copying: a Follow Path-style attachment {track, distance 0..1, orient, offset} and state-machine triggers. As a runtime it is the wrong source of truth, because the geometry is authored in the Rive editor rather than solved by the engine. It also costs at least 222 KB, rasterises to canvas, and needs a paid plan to export. At most, consider it for one self-contained micro-animation.

findings.item: Lottie / dotLottie
findings.facts: The Lottie Animation Community (Linux Foundation / JDF) published the Lottie v1.0 JSON specification on 17 September 2024. dotlottie-web (MIT, npm 0.81.0, 2026-10-06) is a Rust and WASM core on ThorVG with Canvas2D, WebGL2 and experimental WebGPU renderers. It has a Web Worker and OffscreenCanvas option, and state machines built into the file. Theming slots override colour, scalar, vector, gradient, text and image values at runtime, and the README doesn't mention SVG output. lottie-web (MIT, 5.13.0, 2025-05-21) offers svg, canvas and html renderers.
findings.use_for_engine: It's designed for After Effects-style clips with geometry baked at a fixed composition size. Slots can retune values but can't re-solve a track to a new page size. It isn't suited to the frame. Use it only if the owner ever wants a fixed illustrated vignette.

findings.item: Theatre.js (sequenced parameter animation with a studio)
findings.facts: The README says @theatre/core is Apache-2.0 and @theatre/studio is AGPL-3.0, and that 'your project's final bundle only includes @theatre/core'. It animates any JS variable through sheet objects with typed props, and the studio offers a keyframe and sequence editor. Status: the README says 'Theatre.js 1.0 is around the corner' and that development moved to a private repo. The last public commit, 2024-04-11, added that notice. The last npm release is 0.7.2 (2024-05-19).
findings.use_for_engine: It is the closest existing model to what the Lab needs: typed parameters plus keyframed sequences, saved as JSON and played by a small core. It has had no public release for about 2.5 years. Build a small timeline into the Lab using the same model (sheet, object, typed props, keyframes, JSON), or use Theatre only inside the Lab and never ship the studio.

findings.item: View Transitions API, same-document (site section and route changes)
findings.facts: BCD: document.startViewTransition Chrome 111, Firefox 144, Safari 18. The options and types parameter: Chrome 125, Firefox 147, Safari 18.2. view-transition-class: Chrome 125, Firefox 144, Safari 18.2. MDN: the old state is a static image and the new state is a live, interactive region. Each view-transition-name gets its own ::view-transition-group. Names must be unique, or the transition is skipped. If the document is hidden when startViewTransition is called, the transition is skipped entirely. Chrome docs: groups animate width, height and transform, and images are 100% width with auto height. 'During this time [the update callback], the page is frozen.' A reduced-motion preference 'doesn't mean the user wants no motion'.
findings.use_for_engine: The site is a Vue Router SPA (Studio, Projects, Marginalia, Newsletter, About), so this is the 'tab change' hook. Keep the frame out of the raster snapshot. A scaled snapshot of hairline engraving would distort line weights when the page height changes. Name the frame layer, set ::view-transition-group(frame){animation:none}, and hide its old image so the live new frame shows. Start the Courier motion after updateCallbackDone, once the new page height is known and the frame has been re-solved.

findings.item: Cross-document and element-scoped View Transitions
findings.facts: BCD: @view-transition (cross-document, multi-page sites) is Chrome 126 and Safari 18.2, and Firefox does not support it. Element.startViewTransition (element-scoped) is Chrome 147 only, per the Chrome blog of 27 March 2026. It runs a transition on one subtree, allows concurrent and nested transitions, 'keeping the rest of the page interactive', and the scope root gets contain: layout during the transition.
findings.use_for_engine: If the site ever leaves the SPA, cross-document transitions cover Chrome and Safari, and Firefox just changes pages instantly. Element-scoped transitions on <main> are the cleanest way to transition only the content while the frame runs its own vector motion. Treat that as a progressive enhancement in Chrome only.

findings.item: Page Visibility API (switching browser tabs)
findings.facts: MDN calls it Baseline Widely available since July 2015 (visibilitychange: Chrome 62, Firefox 56, Safari 14.1). visibilityState is 'visible' or 'hidden', where hidden means a background tab, a minimised window or the screen off. 'Most browsers stop sending requestAnimationFrame() callbacks to background tabs.' Timers are throttled, using budget-based throttling after 30 s in Firefox and 10 s in Chrome. View transitions are skipped while hidden.
findings.use_for_engine: On hidden: pause the MotionDirector and finish any running motion instantly (commit its end state). On visible: optionally play one short 'return' motion, such as a Courier or a pulse, but rate-limit it, for example only after more than 60 s away (my suggestion). Never queue motions while hidden.

findings.item: prefers-reduced-motion and WCAG
findings.facts: BCD prefers-reduced-motion: Chrome 74, Firefox 63, Safari 10.1. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A) applies to moving content that starts automatically, lasts more than 5 s and is shown alongside other content. It must have a pause, stop or hide mechanism, and decorative motion is not exempt. SC 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (Level AAA): motion triggered by interaction must be possible to disable, with techniques C39/SCR40 (prefers-reduced-motion). Colour and opacity changes are not motion animation.
findings.use_for_engine: Design rule: every motion is triggered by an event and finishes in under 5 s, with no infinite ambient loops. With reduced motion, swap travel or growth for opacity-only versions, and offer a site 'still engraving' toggle stored per viewer. Read it with matchMedia plus a change listener so the setting updates live.

findings.item: Cost of many SVG nodes vs Canvas vs WebGL
findings.facts: Horak, Kister and Dachselt, 'Comparing Rendering Performance of Common Web Technologies for Large Graphs' (IEEE VIS 2018 poster), measured FPS during interaction. SVG (D3) and Canvas performed almost the same. All three lost performance above 400 nodes, about 8,000 graphical elements. WebGL (PixiJS) without text held 50 FPS at about 8 million elements. Research file 04 already warns that animated feTurbulence/feDisplacementMap is CPU-heavy and has crashed Safari on iOS.
findings.use_for_engine: The frame stays SVG and stays static. Only a small motion overlay changes per frame (one glyph, a few dash windows, one re-solved subgraph). Keep animated elements to tens, not thousands, and never animate filters. Consider Canvas or WebGL only if a future effect needs thousands of lines moving at once, such as a full-page guilloché moiré.

findings.item: Supporting CSS: @property, linear() easing, the d property, scroll-driven timelines
findings.facts: @property is Baseline 2024 (July 2024), and typed custom properties interpolate. linear() easing: Chrome 113, Firefox 112, Safari 17.2. The CSS 'd' property, path(): Chrome 52, Firefox 97, Safari not supported. animation-timeline (scroll and view): Chrome 115, Safari 26, Firefox preview only (all BCD).
findings.use_for_engine: Use @property (for example --u as a <number>) only where one CSS variable fans out to many dash windows. Use linear() to ship custom 'engine-like' easing curves designed in the Lab. Don't morph geometry with CSS 'd' because Safari lacks it, so change shapes with JS setAttribute('d'). Scroll-linked tracks are a later, optional idea.

findings.item: Real examples of tasteful line-art and ornament motion
findings.facts: (1) Polygon's PS4 and Xbox One reviews (2013). Illustrator-traced console line art drew itself in with dash animation, and the team chose JS timing over CSS transitions so animations could be chained (Vox Product Blog, archived). (2) Codrops 'SVG Drawing Animation' (30 Dec 2013): line art draws in and then fades into the finished illustration. (3) Codrops 'Animated SVG Frame Slideshow' (15 Nov 2017): an SVG frame morphs on each slide change (anime.js), the closest precedent to 'the frame reacts when you change section'. (4) Vivus: delayed, sync and oneByOne draw-in modes plus per-path scenario timing. (5) Colloseus's calligraphy writing-on (CSS-Tricks 2018). (6) Magic UI AnimatedBeam (MIT): a glow 'travels' along a connector, but the source moves a userSpaceOnUse linearGradient along x only and rebuilds the path with ResizeObserver.
findings.use_for_engine: Take three lessons. Ordering is what makes draw-in elegant (oneByOne, scenarios), and the engine's attachment graph supplies that order. Frame motion on section change has a precedent and reads as deliberate. A glow made by sliding a gradient is not an arc-length travel and fails on vertical or curved tracks, which is why the engine's dash-window or WAAPI sampler is needed.

gaps.recommendation:
ARCHITECTURE: "Motion is time-varying parameters on the same solved graph."
1) One source of truth. A Motion is data in the frame spec, edited in the Lab like any other relationship: {id, trigger (firstVisit | routeChange | visibilityReturn | bandChange), target (a parameter path in the attachment graph, e.g. courier.u, weave.left.phasePacket, flame.growthK, element.reveal), from/to, duration, easing (linear() string), order rule}. Motion state is always stored relative to tracks (normalised arc length u, or s anchored to a socket), never in pixels. A resize then just re-solves geometry and keeps u.
2) Build these hooks into M1 now, though motion ships later. Every curve exposes length, pointAt(s), tangentAt(s) and curvatureAt(s). Rendered pieces get stable IDs and their s-range on the parent track. RibbonPieces keep over/under z-order and halo. The attachment graph exports a topological order. Rendering has two layers: a static engraving SVG and a small motion overlay. Moving parts are a <g transform> or an HTML wrapper, never a <use x= y=>, because Chromium refuses to composite those.
3) A MotionDirector, the single runtime, picks the cheapest tier that is correct:
- Tier A, compositor (rigid travellers and cross-fades): sample the track at uniform s, then element.animate() transform keyframes with offset = s/L. Effect easing sets the speed profile. Only transform and opacity are animated, so the motion stays smooth while Vue mounts the new route.
- Tier B, paint (reveals and pulses): pathLength=1 on spines. Animate stroke-dashoffset dash windows. Filled outlines get mask-reveal per RibbonPiece with the offset shifted by the piece's start s, so motion flows across crossings and is hidden where the strand passes under.
- Tier C, geometry (true shape changes): one rAF loop driven by the timestamp. Re-evaluate only the subgraph downstream of the animated parameter, write only changed 'd' attributes, and keep a frame budget (for example 4 ms; my number, measure it in the Lab). If over budget, fall back to Tier B or A.
Lifecycle: pause and commit end states on visibilitychange→hidden. Use matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') with a change listener plus a per-viewer 'still engraving' toggle that swaps each motion for its opacity variant. Every motion is finite and under 5 s, with no ambient loops. On resize: if a motion is running, finish it instantly, re-solve, rebuild the WAAPI keyframes, or restore currentTime for long ones. Don't animate the resize itself. When the page crosses a design threshold (a different band: 2-ribbon vs 3-strand plait, medallion variant), cross-fade for about 250 ms and never morph across a topology change. Integer repeat refits (fitRepeats) are also discontinuous, so cross-fade those too.
Section change: run a same-document View Transition for the content only. Keep the frame out of the raster snapshot (::view-transition-group(frame){animation:none} with the old image hidden, or Chrome 147's element-scoped transition on <main>). After updateCallbackDone, re-solve the frame for the new page height, then fire the route-change motions. Skip motions while the document is hidden.
4) The Lab gets a timeline lane per Motion (a small Theatre.js-style model: typed params, keyframes, JSON). It has scrub and replay, a reduced-motion preview, a contact sheet at several page sizes playing the same motion, and an ms-per-frame meter for each tier.
VOCABULARY (rudimentary but elegant). Every motion is driven by geometry the engine already has.
- Construction Replay, first visit only. Dominant curves draw in first. Each dependent starts when its parent's pen passes the dependent's attach parameter t, so the order comes from the attachment graph and the relationships become visible. Total about 1.2 to 2 s. Reduced motion: a 300 ms fade.
- Courier, the owner's arrows, on section change. The dart glyph leaves its medallion socket, rides its ribbon strand down the side at constant arc-length speed (Tier A), is hidden under crossings by an overlay mask cut from the over-piece halos, and docks at the far corner. About 0.9 to 1.6 s, scaled to track length with a cap. Reduced motion: no travel, a soft opacity blink at the destination socket.
- Ink Pulse, an alternative to the Courier. A short dark segment travels inside the double-line ribbon through dash windows on each piece (Tier B), occluded correctly at crossings.
- Ripple: one phase packet travels down the weave, ψ(s,t) = A·g((s - v·t)/σ). Crossings slide and then settle, and the ends stay locked to the medallion sockets (Tier C).
- Unfurl: flame leaves appear in growth order, k = 0 to N, under the spiral similarity, each scaling from its base along the log-spiral spine. This shows off the golden construction.
- Rose-engine Turn: rotate one guilloché band by a multiple of 2π/lobes. The end state is identical, and a moiré blooms once along the way. It is a transform, so it is composited.
- Settle: a threshold cross-fade.
Durations can come from a phi token scale (0.38, 0.62, 1, 1.62 s), honestly framed as a token scale with no perceptual claim. Easing should feel like a printing or engraving machine: near-constant velocity with short ease-in and ease-out, not springs or bounces.
cautions: Chromium does not composite offset-path/offset-distance animations (they are not on the compositable-property list in compositor_animations.cc), so CSS Motion Path runs on the main thread and can stutter during route renders. Use WAAPI transform keyframes for travellers.

Chromium refuses composited transform animations on <use> elements with x/y and on symbol or viewBox containers. The current engine places ornaments that way (src/frames/frameEngine.ts:210, framing/render/svg.ts:38), so wrap moving parts in <g transform> or an HTML wrapper.
Elements inside SVG masks or clipPaths are never composited, and stroke-dashoffset always repaints, so Tier B reveals run on the main thread. Keep them few and short.

I could not confirm that Safari composites transform animations on SVG child elements (WebKit's LBSE is not the default as far as I found). The cross-engine composited option is a small HTML-level wrapper.

offset-path: path() takes px only and won't follow a re-solved frame. I have not verified that url() follows live 'd' changes; test it in the Lab. shape() support is new (Baseline February 2026), and BCD doesn't separate offset-path support from clip-path.
The CSS 'd' property is unsupported in Safari, so shape morphs need JS setAttribute.

View Transition snapshots of the old state are raster images that stretch when the page height changes, which would distort hairline engraving. Keep the frame out of the snapshot. The page is frozen during the update callback, so start frame motion after it.
Cross-document View Transitions are not supported in Firefox. Element-scoped transitions are Chrome 147 only.
rAF stops in background tabs. Compute progress from timestamps, which matters on 120/144 Hz screens, and don't queue motions while hidden.
WCAG 2.2.2 (Level A) applies to auto-starting motion over 5 s alongside content, decorative or not. Avoid ambient loops entirely, or add a pause control.

The GSAP licence is proprietary to Webflow and can be amended or terminated. It prohibits, without consent, use in no-code visual animation tools that compete with Webflow, which is uncomfortably close to a shared Frame Lab.

Rive exports have needed a paid plan since 20 Oct 2025, the smallest web runtime is about 222 KB brotli, it renders to canvas, and its geometry is authored in Rive, not solved by the engine. Lottie also bakes geometry at authoring time.
Theatre.js has had no public release since 0.7.2 (19 May 2024), and its studio is AGPL-3.0.
Integer repeat counts (weave periods, scallops) change in steps as the page resizes. Don't animate through them; cross-fade or snap.
Duration numbers, the 4 ms budget and the 'return after more than 60 s' rule are my design suggestions, not sourced figures. Measure them in the Lab.
The SVG vs Canvas data (Horak 2018) is older and measured whole-scene redraws. It supports keeping the animated set small; it does not give exact limits for 2026 browsers.

gaps.summary: Map styling, cartographic generalisation, type design, icon systems and CSS have each worked out how the room available decides which design to show, and they agree on one model. (1) A single continuous size input is measured on a log scale: map zoom doubles per level; optical size is measured in points; Chaparral's optical-size ranges and Android's size classes grow by ratios. (2) Each property declares whether it may vary continuously (interpolate) or only in steps (step), and whether it is fixed. MapLibre's spec stores this per property: about 80 of its 146 layout and paint properties are interpolable, and the rest are step-only, cross-faded or constant. (3) A few designer-drawn masters or anchors are interpolated between, but only while their structure is compatible. SF Symbols builds 27 variants from 3 masters, and those masters must have the same number of paths and control points. When structure has to change, a discrete swap fires at a threshold instead. OpenType's 'rvrn' feature does this: a dollar sign loses a stroke at heavy weights, and the trigger values should sit midway between named instances. (4) Elements have visibility ranges with an inclusive minimum and exclusive maximum, a priority for resolving collisions, and optional parts that can drop out. Cartographers apply changes in a fixed order: content, then geometry, then symbol, then label. Töpfer's radical law and tippecanoe's drop rate show that element counts fall more slowly than size. (5) Flicker is handled with hysteresis margins or fades (Godot), by making sure the decoration can never change the box it measures (container queries query only ancestors; the ResizeObserver depth rule), and by `scrollbar-gutter: stable`. (6) Designers see every threshold at once. ScaleMaster is a chart with log-scale on the horizontal axis, one row per feature, and bars showing which design applies at each scale. Polypane's "Breakpoint Edges" shows panes just below and above each breakpoint. Mapbox Studio and Maputnik edit a value-versus-zoom curve as a table of stops. The ratios between adjacent design sizes in these systems range from 1.28 (SF Symbols) to 2.0 (map zoom), and φ (1.618) falls inside that range. For the frame, the "zoom" should be a room level measured per ornament slot, not the viewport width.

findings.item: MapLibre style-spec expressions: step, interpolate, match, case, coalesce, and the zoom restriction
findings.facts: step: ["step", input, output_0, stop_1, out_1, ...] returns the output of the last stop below the input, or output_0 when the input is below the first stop. Stop inputs must be numeric literals in strictly ascending order. interpolate supports ["linear"], ["exponential", base] (base above 1 makes the output rise towards the high end, near 1 is linear) and ["cubic-bezier", x1, y1, x2, y2] (x in 0..1 keeps it monotonic, y may overshoot). It outputs a number, a colour or an array; interpolate-hcl and interpolate-lab exist for colour. match: labels must be unique, with a fallback. case: the first true condition wins. coalesce: the first non-null value. Restriction: ["zoom"] may only be the input to a top-level (outer) step or interpolate, optionally wrapped in let.
findings.use_for_engine: Use a small JSON subset of this grammar for room rules: step, interpolate (linear, exponential, cubic-bezier), match, case, coalesce and let/var. Keep the restriction that the room input may only drive a top-level step or interpolate. My inference, not stated by the spec: that restriction is what makes every rule a list of stops a tool can read, so the lab can always draw it as a graph or bar chart instead of opaque code.

findings.item: MapLibre per-property typing: interpolable vs step-only vs cross-faded vs constant (v8.json)
findings.facts: Each property carries expression.interpolated (true or false), its allowed parameters (zoom, feature) and a property-type. The types are: data-driven ('interpolable and can be represented using a property expression'), cross-faded ('non-interpolable; rather, its values will be cross-faded to smoothly transition between integer zooms', used for line-dasharray, line-pattern and fill-pattern), data-constant, constant ('constant across all zoom levels') and color-ramp. My count from the file: of 146 layout and paint properties, 80 are interpolated:true and 65 are false. symbol-sort-key, text-optional, text-variable-anchor and symbol-placement are step-only. Seamless line and fill patterns need image widths that are a factor of two.
findings.use_for_engine: Give every frame parameter a declared kind: continuous (stroke weights, swing amplitude, spacing, ring radius), discrete (leaf count, fan line count, plait vs twist, which motif variant), grow (discrete, with a transition band) or locked (φ constants, which may not take a room expression at all). The lab draws a curve editor for continuous parameters and bars for discrete ones. A validator refuses interpolate on a discrete parameter.

findings.item: Mapbox: paint properties re-evaluated continuously, layout properties once per integer zoom
findings.facts: Quoted from the Mapbox spec's legacy 'functions' section: 'Paint properties are continuously re-evaluated whenever the zoom level changes, even fractionally.' 'Layout properties, however, are evaluated only once for each integer zoom level.' Stops are [zoom, value] pairs, and base is the exponential base (default 1, linear). Zoom and property functions are deprecated in favour of expressions.
findings.use_for_engine: Use the same split. Structure (topology, element counts, which elements exist) is decided at discrete room levels and cached. Cheap appearance parameters (weights, offsets, amplitudes) vary continuously. Expensive geometry is then rebuilt only when the structure changes or the room crosses a quantisation step.

findings.item: MapLibre layer visibility ranges and symbol collision and priority rules
findings.facts: minzoom is inclusive ('At zoom levels less than the minzoom, the layer will be hidden'). maxzoom is exclusive ('equal to or greater than the maxzoom... hidden'). symbol-sort-key: 'Features with lower sort keys are drawn and placed first... will have priority during placement' (from v8.json). text-optional and icon-optional let one half of a label+icon pair survive when the other collides. text-variable-anchor tries anchor positions in order before giving up. text-padding and icon-padding (default 2 px, interpolable) enlarge collision boxes. text-overlap is never, always or cooperative. symbol-spacing defaults to 250 px along lines. Map options (https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/API/type-aliases/MapOptions): fadeDuration, default 300 ms, fades label-collision changes. crossSourceCollisions defaults to true.
findings.use_for_engine: Each ornament element gets minRoom (inclusive), maxRoom (exclusive), a priority, an optional flag and an ordered list of fallback placements or forms. When two elements compete for a corner, the lower priority yields first: optional leaves drop before the stem they hang on. Padding gives a minimum clearance in CSS px around motifs. A short fade (or the engraving-style grow-in) smooths collision-driven changes.

findings.item: Mapbox Studio authoring of zoom-dependent values
findings.facts: 'Style across zoom range': 'Values can be specified for any number of stops at any specified zoom level.' The rate-of-change options are linear (default), exponential (a custom base), cubic-bezier and step ('discrete, stepped results'). Other modes are 'Style with data conditions' and 'Style across data range'. A layer's 'Zoom extent' sets its min and max zoom. Mapbox patent US10416866B2 (https://patents.google.com/patent/US10416866, priority 2016, granted 2019, listed expiry 2037) describes this editor: a graph of property value against zoom with a rate-of-change control, value editors with an 'add stop' button, and one live map re-rendered at the selected zoom.
findings.use_for_engine: The per-parameter editor should be a value-versus-room graph with draggable stops, a rate-of-change dropdown (linear, exponential base, cubic-bezier, step) and a live preview at the scrubbed room level. The patent exists and covers this editor style. This is not legal advice, but the owner should know about it before publishing a public tool.

findings.item: Maputnik (open-source MapLibre editor): zoom-function UI
findings.facts: From the source code (the wiki pages are nearly empty): every zoom-capable property has a button, 'Convert property into a zoom function' (FunctionButtons.tsx). It opens a 'Stops' table with columns Zoom (an input clamped to 0..22) and Output value, a delete button per row, a Base field, an 'Add stop' button and a 'Convert to expression' escape hatch to raw JSON. Stops are re-sorted by zoom on every edit.
findings.use_for_engine: This is a simple, proven UX for a non-programmer. Any parameter can be promoted from a constant to room-dependent with one click, then edited as a small sorted table of stops, with raw JSON available only as an escape hatch. Keep that progression: constant, then stops table, then expression.

findings.item: ScaleMaster (Brewer and Buttenfield): designing for the whole scale range at once
findings.facts: In a graduate exercise, maps for 1:10K to 1:5M were designed by sampling progressively smaller scales (for example 13K, 20K, 45K, 150K, 300K, 600K, 1M, 4M) and critiquing them as a group. Students then adjusted 'visibility ranges, eliminating subsets of features, and adjusting symbols'. 'The focus was not on designing for the anchor scale... the group was designing for the entire range.' The diagram: feature groups down the side, scale on a logarithmic axis (drawn on graph paper), horizontal bars for the range in which each representation is used, and letters at break points noting the change (for example, at about 1:150K main rivers are selected from the 1:100K data and lake outlines lightened). Bars that stop mean the feature is eliminated. Symbol change combined with selection 'can produce maps through almost the entire range of scales'. The journal version is in Cartography and Geographic Information Science 34(1), 2007, per search results (not opened).
findings.use_for_engine: This is the main threshold view for the Frame Lab. Each slot gets a ScaleMaster strip with elements and discrete parameters as rows, the room level as a log x-axis, coloured bars for each variant's range, draggable break points and short notes at each break. The sampling-and-critique loop maps onto an auto-generated filmstrip at chosen room levels.

findings.item: Typology of multi-scale operators (Roth, Brewer and Stryker 2011)
findings.facts: This builds on ScaleMaster with 24 operators in four groups. Content: add, eliminate, reclassify, reorder. Geometry: aggregate, collapse, merge, displace, exaggerate, simplify, smooth. Symbol: adjust colour, pattern, size, shape, transparency and iconicity, plus enhance, rotate, and typify (replace a set with a sparser representative arrangement). Label: add, eliminate, adjust appearance, adjust position. Multi-scale design usually proceeds content, then geometry, then symbol, then label, and iterates. At intermediate scales, legibility can sometimes be kept with content and symbol changes alone.
findings.use_for_engine: Use this as the vocabulary for what a threshold may do: add or eliminate an element, typify (fewer loops, beads or leaves in the same pattern), collapse (a double-line ribbon becomes a single rule), simplify (fewer fan lines), exaggerate (thicken a hairline), enhance (add hatch). Evaluate per slot in the same order: which elements exist, then their topology and geometry, then weights, then collision resolution.

findings.item: Töpfer's radical law (principle of selection)
findings.facts: Jiang, Liu and Jia (arXiv, drafts 2011-2013) restate Töpfer and Pillewizer (1966): N_d = N_s · sqrt(M_s / M_d), where N is the number of objects and M the scale denominators. Halving the scale does not halve the count; the retained fraction follows the square root. They note its limits: it 'indicates how many objects should be selected, but it does not come up with which ones'. They propose ranking by a head/tail split instead.
findings.use_for_engine: My analogy, not a source claim: when a rail or fan loses room by a factor k, the reduction can be split between element size and element count, not taken all from one. The radical law suggests count ∝ sqrt(k), so elements also shrink by about sqrt(k). Expose this as one dial (size-vs-count split α, with α=0.5 as the radical-law preset). Pair it with an explicit priority order that decides which elements go.

findings.item: tippecanoe: concrete per-zoom LOD rules, and the 'texture' philosophy
findings.facts: Lines and polygons are Douglas-Peucker simplified to tile resolution at every zoom. For points, it 'keeps only 1/2.5 of the dots for each zoom level below the... base zoom'; the author writes that densities of many datasets 'fall off at about this same rate'. -r sets the rate. Gamma thins clusters closer than one pixel (gamma 2 gives the square root). Tiny polygons are probabilistically merged so total area is preserved. The stated intent is a scale-independent view that keeps 'the density and texture of the data' rather than dropping 'supposedly unimportant features'. The zoom table halves the scale denominator per level (z7 is about 1:2,500,000, z8 about 1:1,250,000).
findings.use_for_engine: For engraved line families (hatch, lattice, beads, fans), keep the texture: hold the physical pitch in CSS px or device px roughly constant and change counts, rather than scaling pitch with the frame. Give lines below a device-pixel gap a rule: merge or drop by priority. This agrees with the priority-tier idea already in 04-engraving-print.md.

findings.item: Responsive Logos (Joe Harrison, 2014) and responsive SVG icons
findings.facts: 'An exploration into scalable logos for the modern web. Resize your browser (Or rotate your device) to see the reductions based on screen size.' Concept by Joe Harrison, 2014; a personal experiment. Its style.css (https://responsivelogos.co.uk/style.css) uses one SVG sprite per logo with 300 px frames (offsets 0, -300, -600, -900), switched by viewport min-width media queries at 15em, 28em, 45em and 60em, so four discrete variants tied to the viewport, not the logo's box. Kottke (https://kottke.org/tag/Joe%20Harrison) describes logos that 'lose detail and become more abstract' down to the Disney 'D' or the Nike swoosh. Smashing Magazine, 'Rethinking Responsive SVG' (https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2014/03/rethinking-responsive-svg/), puts all variants in one SVG as groups shown by media queries inside the SVG. Media queries in an SVG loaded via img did not work in the author's tests; object did.
findings.use_for_engine: This is the discrete-variant baseline: a few hand-designed reductions, each keeping the most recognisable core. For the frame that core is the medallion's ring and S-sweep, then the stems, then fans and leaves. Unlike Harrison's version, select on the slot's own room, not the viewport, and generate rather than store the variants.

findings.item: SF Symbols: 9 weights × 3 scales built from 3 masters, explicit overrides, compatibility rule
findings.facts: HIG (https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sf-symbols): nine weights matched to the San Francisco font, and three scales (small, medium default, large) 'defined relative to the cap height'. Custom symbols: a variable template has 3 sets of paths (Ultralight-S, Regular-S, Black-S), 'the minimum number of variants necessary for the system to generate the other 24' by vector interpolation. A static template has 27. Interpolation requires the three sources to be path-based with 'the same number of paths and the same number of control points'. 'If they're present, the system uses them instead of interpolation', so explicit variants override. Scale factors are S 0.783, M 1.0, L 1.29. Each variant can have its own margins, falling back to interpolated margins. SF Symbols 7 adds Draw On and Draw Off, which draw a symbol 'along a path through a set of guide points' (relevant later for the animation idea).
findings.use_for_engine: Use the masters + interpolation + overrides model. The designer sets a few anchor parameter sets (for example small, medium and large room); the engine interpolates continuous parameters between anchors only while discrete parameters agree, which is the compatibility rule. The designer can pin a hand-tuned override at any room level, and the override wins over interpolation. Per-variant margins correspond to per-variant clearance and padding.

findings.item: Icon systems redraw per size, with a constant screen stroke
findings.facts: GitHub Primer Octicons: 'Always design two versions of each icon: a 16px version and a 24px version.' 'Use a consistent stroke width of 1.5px for both.' 12px is drawn only for a specific need. Material Symbols (https://developers.google.com/fonts/docs/material_symbols) is a variable icon font with FILL 0..1, wght 100..700, GRAD and opsz 20..48 dp: 'Optical size offers a way to automatically adjust the stroke weight when you increase or decrease the symbol size.' The page is inconsistent about the default opsz.
findings.use_for_engine: Line weights should be specified in screen units with floors (for example hairline ≥ 0.5-0.75 CSS px, per 04-engraving-print.md), not scaled with the ornament. Smaller rooms therefore get relatively heavier, simpler line work, as icon optical sizes do.

findings.item: OpenType optical-size axis (opsz): selection rules
findings.facts: 'Used to vary design to suit different text sizes'; values are text size in points. 'Applications may choose to select an optical-size variant automatically based on the displayed text size.' Selection should follow size 'as seen by the reader', including viewing distance. 'Types of zoom that do not trigger re-layout of text should not change Optical size variant selection.' Outside the axis range, selection 'should be clamped to the appropriate minimum or maximum axis value, not reset to the default'. Software should provide a means to override automatic selection. Google Fonts Knowledge (https://github.com/google/fonts/blob/main/cc-by-sa/knowledge/glossary/terms/optical_size_axis/content.md) notes that browsers match opsz to CSS px, not points. Small optical sizes have less contrast, wider spacing and a taller x-height.
findings.use_for_engine: Three rules carry over directly. Pinch-zoom must not change the frame variant: MDN confirms pinch-zoom leaves devicePixelRatio and CSS px unchanged, while browser zoom changes both and so triggers relayout. Clamp the room level at the ends of the designed range rather than falling back to a default. Allow a per-page manual override of the variant.

findings.item: How type designers distribute optical masters (Chaparral Pro)
findings.facts: Adobe's Chaparral Pro release notes give the ranges Caption 6-8.3 pt, Regular 8.4-12.9, Subhead 13-25.9, Display 26+. At larger sizes, letter fit tightens, counters close, serifs become finer, contrast rises, weight lightens and the x-height diminishes; at smaller sizes the opposite. 'The difference in design between the Chaparral Pro Caption and Regular optical sizes, which may have a difference in size of only 4 points, is almost as much as the difference between the regular and display sizes, which have a difference of 10-60 points.' Ahrens and Mugikura, Size-specific adjustments to type designs (https://justanotherfoundry.com/size-specific-adjustments-to-type-designs): small sizes 'typically show an increased width and x-height, reduced stroke contrast and looser spacing'.
findings.use_for_engine: Space thresholds on a log scale and put more of them, with bigger design changes, at the small end. Chaparral's range boundaries step by ×1.40, ×1.55 and ×2.0. For the frame, the phone-size corner needs the most design attention, and the desktop variants can share one master.

findings.item: OpenType 'rvrn' and FeatureVariations: discrete swaps inside a continuous design space
findings.facts: Interpolated variants of a glyph 'have exactly the same contours and points'. Making 'significant outline changes, such as reducing strokes in heavy-weight' variants by interpolation 'can be difficult... and might not produce desired results', so the glyph is substituted for a different one under condition sets on axis ranges. Example: a dollar sign with two full vertical strokes becomes one stroke at Bold, and bars only at top and bottom at Black. 'The axis values used to trigger a condition should normally be midway between values used for named instances.'
findings.use_for_engine: This is the core hybrid rule. Within a topology class, interpolate. When the structure must change (fewer flame leaves, 3-strand plait to 2-ribbon twist, a medallion collapsing to a simple corner, a fan going from 6 to 4 lines), use a discrete switch on a room range. By default, place each switch at the log-midpoint between the two adjacent designed anchors.

findings.item: CSS container queries, container units, clamp()
findings.facts: container-type: size (inline and block axes, applies layout, style and size containment), inline-size (inline axis only), normal (style and name queries only). Queryable size features are width, height, inline-size, block-size, aspect-ratio and orientation (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_containment/Container_size_and_style_queries). Units cqw, cqh, cqi, cqb, cqmin and cqmax are 1% of the container's dimension; with no eligible container they fall back to small-viewport units. Style queries currently support custom properties only. The query container is selected 'from among the element's ancestor query containers' (W3C CSS Containment 3, Working Draft 18 Aug 2022, https://www.w3.org/TR/css-contain-3/). clamp(MIN, VAL, MAX) = max(MIN, min(VAL, MAX)) (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/clamp).
findings.use_for_engine: Let CSS own the page layout and reserve the slots: gutters, masthead height and band thickness, set by container or media queries and clamp(). The engine only measures each slot and fills it. Keep the ancestor-only rule: an ornament never queries or resizes its own box. The engine can publish its chosen variant back as a custom property (for example --frame-corner: 'medallion-s') so CSS style queries can adapt nearby typography.

findings.item: Feedback loops and layout jitter: ResizeObserver depth rule, scrollbar-gutter, devicePixelRatio
findings.facts: Resize events run before paint; if any fire, layout is re-evaluated. 'Infinite loops from cyclic dependencies are addressed by only processing elements deeper in the DOM during each iteration', and otherwise 'ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications' fires. This 'only prevents user-agent lockup, not the infinite loop itself', and users may see 'a flash of broken layout'. The suggested fixes are to defer to requestAnimationFrame or track an expected size. scrollbar-gutter: stable reserves the scrollbar's space to avoid 'unneeded layout changes' as scrollbars appear (Baseline 2024, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scrollbar-gutter). devicePixelRatio changes with page zoom but not pinch-zoom; watch it with matchMedia('(resolution: Xdppx)') (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/devicePixelRatio).
findings.use_for_engine: Render the frame as an absolutely positioned, pointer-events:none layer that never feeds size back into layout. Set scrollbar-gutter: stable on the root so content growth cannot flip the width across a threshold. Treat devicePixelRatio as an input for hairline LOD only, re-read through matchMedia.

findings.item: Godot visibility ranges: hysteresis margins, fade modes, hierarchical LOD
findings.facts: Each instance has Begin and End distances plus Begin and End Margins, documented as 'the hysteresis or alpha fade transition distance'. Fade mode 'Disabled' 'uses hysteresis to switch between LOD levels instantly' and is fastest. 'Self' fades the node out over the margin; 'Dependencies' fades in its children (hierarchical LOD). Fade mode only matters when a margin is above 0. A 'Visibility Parent' hides child nodes while the parent's coarse representation is visible; a node cannot use its own child as its parent, which would be a dependency cycle.
findings.use_for_engine: Each discrete switch gets a margin (a Schmitt trigger): switch up at t·φ^(+h) and down at t·φ^(−h). Choose instant or faded per parameter. The Visibility Parent idea fits the attachment graph: when the simplified corner variant is active, its whole subtree of fans and leaves is hidden as one unit, and dependents never decide their own visibility.

findings.item: Android window size classes: few, opinionated, available-space-based classes
findings.facts: Width classes: Compact <600 dp, Medium 600-840, Expanded 840-1200, Large 1200-1600, Extra-large ≥1600. Height classes: <480, 480-900, ≥900. These are 'opinionated viewport breakpoints'. They 'are explicitly not determined by the size of the device screen' and are 'not intended for isTablet-type logic'. 'available width is usually more important than available height due to the ubiquity of vertical scrolling.' The class can change at runtime.
findings.use_for_engine: Use two tiers. A few page-level width classes (CSS) decide which slots exist: no side gutters on phones means the rails move or vanish, and the garland might run along the bottom only. Per-slot room levels then decide variants inside each slot. Page height should mostly drive counts (rail length), not variant choice.

findings.item: Polypane: previewing every breakpoint and its edges
findings.facts: It 'automatically detects width-based CSS media query breakpoints defined in your CSS' and can open a pane per breakpoint. 'Breakpoint Edges help you find edge cases by creating panes for the breakpoint and the size right below or above it.' The 'Simplified' option groups breakpoints 'into five different buckets and create[s] a pane of the average of each bucket'. The page does not mention container queries.
findings.use_for_engine: The Frame Lab's filmstrip should be generated from the rules, not chosen by hand: one cell per designed anchor, one pair of cells at the two edges of each threshold (just below and just above, including the hysteresis band), and one cell per clamped extreme.

findings.item: Rive N-Slicing: fixed corners, stretch/repeat/hidden edges (prior art for frames)
findings.facts: An N-Slice starts with 4 axes and 9 segments; axes are in points or percentages, and more can be added. Segments alternate, 'starting with a fixed segment'. Scaling segments can be Stretch, Repeat or Hidden, but 'Tile modes can only be changed on image/raster based n-slices', so vector groups only stretch.
findings.use_for_engine: This confirms the frame decomposition into fixed corners and repeating rails. It also shows the gap the engine fills: vector stretching distorts circles and spirals (see 01-curve-systems.md on affine invariance). The engine instead re-solves rails with whole-number repeats and swaps corner variants by room.

gaps.recommendation:
ROOM-DEPENDENT ORNAMENT MODEL (my synthesis from the sources above; the numeric defaults are proposals, not sourced values)

1. The frame's "zoom" is a room level measured per slot, not the viewport width.
- Slots: corner, side rail, top/bottom band, crest, tailpiece. CSS owns page layout and reserves each slot using a few page width classes (for example compact <600, medium 600-1200, wide ≥1200 CSS px, following Android's classes), media or container queries, and clamp(). The engine measures each slot with ResizeObserver and fills it. It must never change the size it measures (the ancestor-only rule and the ResizeObserver depth rule). Set scrollbar-gutter: stable on the root.
- Per-slot inputs:
  - z = log_φ(s / sRef), where s is the slot's governing size in CSS px (corner: min(w, h); rail: gutter width; band: band height) and sRef is that size at drawing scale 1. One z step is ×1.618. In the sourced systems, adjacent design sizes differ by ×1.28 to ×2.0 (SF Symbols 1.28-1.29, Android 1.33-1.43, Chaparral 1.4-2.0, Primer 1.5, Responsive Logos 1.33-1.87, map zoom 2.0), so a φ ladder is ordinary, not exotic.
  - aspect = w/h.
  - length = run length; it drives repeat counts only, never which variant.
  - devPx = device px per design unit (CSS scale × devicePixelRatio); it drives the hairline floor and merging or dropping lines.
  - widthClass, from CSS.
- Pinch-zoom never changes the variant; browser zoom does, because it relayouts (the opsz rule). Clamp z at the ends of the designed range rather than reverting to a default.

2. Rule language: a JSON subset of MapLibre expressions.
- Operators: step, interpolate (linear, exponential base, cubic-bezier), match, case, coalesce, let/var, plus ['room','z'|'aspect'|'length'|'devPx'] and ['phi', k].
- Room inputs may only drive a top-level step or interpolate, so every rule stays a readable list of stops that the lab can draw.
- Every parameter declares a kind, as in MapLibre's property-type:
  - continuous: interpolate allowed (weights, swing, spacing, radii, fan spread).
  - discrete: step only (leaf count, fan line count, plait/twist, motif variant, collapse ribbon to rule).
  - grow: discrete, but new lines are born from zero width across the hysteresis band, which suits engraving better than an opacity fade (my judgment).
  - locked: φ constants, no room expression allowed.
- Sketch:
  - `type ParamKind = 'continuous' | 'discrete' | 'grow' | 'locked'`
  - `type ParamSpec = { id; kind; unit; min?; max?; value: Expr }`
  - `type ElementRule = { id; parent?; minZ? /*inclusive*/; maxZ? /*exclusive*/; priority; optional?; fallback?: ElementId[] }`
  - `type SlotSpec = { id; governs: 'min' | 'width' | 'height'; sRef; hysteresis: number /*z units, default 0.05 ≈ ±2.4% size*/; anchors: { z; params }[]; overrides?: { z; params }[] }`

3. Variants are masters, switches and overrides (the SF Symbols, rvrn and Cecconi LoD anchor patterns).
- The designer authors 2-4 anchor parameter sets per slot, for example z = -1, 0, +1 (S/M/L). Put more of them, and bigger changes, at the small end (Chaparral).
- Continuous parameters interpolate between adjacent anchors only while all discrete parameters agree, which is the compatibility rule.
- Where discrete values differ, the engine inserts a step at the log-midpoint between the anchors (rvrn's "midway" rule); the designer can drag it.
- A pinned override at any z beats interpolation (SF Symbols).
- The lab compiles anchors into expressions automatically. The designer edits anchors and bars, and raw JSON appears only through a "convert to expression" escape hatch (Maputnik).

4. Evaluation per slot runs in Roth et al.'s order: content, then geometry, then symbol, then collisions.
- (a) Which elements exist: minZ/maxZ, with the visibility-parent idea (a collapsed corner hides its whole subtree).
- (b) Topology and discrete parameters, with a Schmitt trigger: up at t·φ^h, down at t·φ^-h; on first load there is no history, so pick canonically at t.
- (c) Continuous parameters.
- (d) Weights with device-px floors (Primer and icon practice: constant screen stroke, so small rooms get relatively heavier, simpler line work).
- (e) Collisions resolved by priority, as with symbol-sort-key: optional parts drop first, fallback forms are tried in order as with variable anchors, and padding sets clearance in CSS px.
- Rails and bands: whole-number repeats. The existing framing/math/phi.ts fitRepeats rounds with no hysteresis and should go through the same trigger. Add an optional size-vs-count split α (α = 0.5 is the radical-law preset) and keep the pitch of line families constant in screen px (tippecanoe's texture idea; the tiers in 04).
- Mirror Mapbox's split between structure (layout) and appearance (paint): topology is recomputed only at discrete changes, continuous parameters on quantised z (for example 1/32 step), and results are cached by (slot, quantised z, variant key).

5. Lab UX for seeing every threshold at once.
- (i) A ScaleMaster strip per slot: rows are elements and discrete parameters, the x-axis is z (log) with ticks at φ steps, and markers show where real devices land (360, 768, 1280 and 1920 px widths mapped into each slot's z). Coloured bars show variant ranges, break points are draggable, and short notes label each break.
- (ii) A filmstrip generated from the rules: each anchor, both edges of each threshold including the hysteresis band (Polypane Breakpoint Edges), and the clamped extremes. Each cell carries validator badges: hairline below floor, gap below device px, collision, stretch, clamp.
- (iii) One large live canvas with a z scrubber, a "sweep" button that animates z from min to max to catch pops, and a toggle between live-resize behaviour (with hysteresis) and canonical behaviour.
- (iv) A curve editor per continuous parameter: value against z, a stops table, and a rate-of-change dropdown (Mapbox Studio / Maputnik).
- (v) The whole-page contact sheet at device sizes already proposed in 06.

6. Transitions now, animation later.
- Discrete changes during live resize are instant by default (Godot's 'Disabled'), or 'grow' for line families.
- MapLibre's 300 ms collision fade is a reasonable ceiling for any fade.
- The later tab-change animation (arrows running along a track) can reuse the same machinery, because parameters are already functions of an input. SF Symbols 7's Draw On along guide points is the nearest shipped precedent.
cautions: I did not open the Mapbox Studio 'More powerful styling' blog post (it returned 403), the 2007 CaGIS ScaleMaster paper (its details come from search results), or the Polypane synced-panes page. The Maputnik UI facts come from its source code because the wiki pages are nearly empty.

Mapbox holds patent US10416866B2 on a zoom-level function graph editor (priority 2016, listed expiry 2037 according to Google Patents). A value-versus-room graph editor in the Frame Lab resembles it. I am not giving legal advice. It is probably irrelevant for a private tool, but the owner should know about it before publishing the lab as a public product.
The 'paint continuous, layout per integer zoom' quote comes from Mapbox's legacy functions docs. I did not confirm that MapLibre keeps exactly the same evaluation rule.

The Responsive Logos level count (4 sprite frames at 15/28/45/60em) is my reading of the site's style.css. The styling below 15em ('center top') is ambiguous, and secondary articles mention 5-6 levels.

These are my proposals, not sourced values: the φ-based room ladder, the default hysteresis (0.05 z, about ±2.4% size), the 1/32-step quantisation, the 'grow-from-zero-width' transition, and the radical-law size-vs-count split for ornaments. The sources only show that adjacent design sizes in real systems differ by ×1.28 to ×2.0.

Hysteresis makes the output depend on resize history, which conflicts with the 'pure function of box size' principle in 05-web-runtime-systems.md. Keep the band small and always choose canonically on load, so that a reload is deterministic.

Never interpolate a discrete quantity (a leaf count or fan line count as a real number). The compatibility rule (same structure on both sides) has to be enforced by the validator, not left to the designer. Otherwise topology 'pops' mid-interpolation.

Too many thresholds become unmaintainable; 06 records the 'spaghetti graph' failure of parametric models. Aim for 2-4 anchors per slot and a handful of page width classes, which is what Android, SF Symbols and Chaparral all do.

CSS cannot compute SVG path geometry. Container queries and cq units can drive only layout reservation and simple CSS-level parameters, so curve generation stays in TypeScript, re-run on ResizeObserver and cached. If it is re-solved on every resize frame without quantisation and caching, it will jank.

Material Symbols' documentation is inconsistent about its default optical size (24 vs 48). The CSS-px-to-opsz browser mapping comes from Google Fonts Knowledge, not from the CSS spec, which I did not open.
The W3C CSS Containment 3 document I read is a 2022 Working Draft. I did not check which current spec hosts container queries.

gaps.summary:
The browser editors that hold up (tldraw, Excalidraw, Figma, Theatre.js, Rive, Graphite, Cuttle) share one pattern. Each has a plain-data document of named records, a small deterministic runtime that turns that document into graphics, and a heavier editor that only produces and changes the document. Theatre.js shows the split most clearly: only @theatre/core ships in the final bundle, while the AGPL studio exports JSON and is gated behind import.meta.env.DEV.

For the owner's "dominant functions with things relative to them," the right core is a directed dependency graph, not a constraint solver. The Cassowary authors say acyclic systems are solved efficiently by local propagation, which is an order of magnitude faster, and recommend cooperating subsolvers. SolveSpace solves groups in sequence and keeps earlier groups fixed. The browser-ready CAD solvers also lack the curves this project needs. planegcs (FreeCAD's solver as WASM, 484 KB, LGPL) offers lines, arcs, conics and B-splines. SolveSpace offers lines, circles, arcs and cubics. Neither has clothoids or log spirals. So solving belongs in three bounded places, all in the Lab or inside one node: drag inversion for handles, small local fits, and an optional bake step.

Incremental recompute is solved: version-stamped, lazy, memoised graphs (Preact Signals, MobX, Solid, tldraw's own signals, the Observable runtime). Persistence lessons are consistent across tools:
- Versioned forward migrations with up/down steps (tldraw).
- Normalise on load and keep unknown fields (Excalidraw restore.ts).
- Keep legacy algorithms addressable so saved art never shifts (Excalidraw ROUNDNESS.LEGACY).
- Accept one major version and ignore unknown minor additions (Rive .riv).
- Write deterministic text for git (Godot TSCN; JCS-style ordering).

Undo should be patch-based (immer patches), grouped into one step per drag with marks and squash, and kept separate from session state (tldraw).

findings.item: Preact Signals: @preact/signals-core and the 'Signal Boosting' implementation article
findings.facts: Core package @preact/signals-core (README at github.com/preactjs/signals packages/core) exports signal, computed, effect, batch, untracked and peek. Its examples are plain JS with no framework. The README says 'Updates flow through computed, but only if someone subscribes to it.' The article describes the algorithm: computeds are evaluated lazily, when read. Each signal has a version number, and there is a global version. A computed returns its cache if the global version is unchanged. Otherwise it re-checks its dependencies in stored order by version and recomputes only if one changed. Its own version increments only if its output actually changed. Dependencies sit in doubly linked lists, with O(1) insert and remove and node reuse across runs. A computed subscribes upstream only while something listens, so unused computeds can be garbage collected. Bundlephobia reports v1.14.4 at 5.5 KB minified, 2.0 KB gzip, with 0 dependencies.
findings.use_for_engine: Copy this version-stamp algorithm for the runtime evaluator: global version, per-node version, ordered re-check of inputs, and no propagation when an output is unchanged. Alternatively, wrap each frame node in a signals-core computed. At about 2 KB it is acceptable inside the shipped runtime.

findings.item: MobX computed values
findings.facts: Computeds 'evaluate lazily, caching their output and only recomputing if one of the underlying observables has changed.' 'If they are not observed by anything, they suspend entirely.' keepAlive prevents suspension but risks leaks. Computeds should have no side effects. The equals option (default Object.is; also compareStructural, compareShallow) stops observers re-running when the output is equal. In the OrderLine example, the autorun does not re-run because the computed 'will detect its output hasn't been affected.'
findings.use_for_engine: Use structural or epsilon equality on geometric outputs. Example: if a resize leaves a spine's resolved points within 1e-6, its dependents do not re-run. Node compute functions must be pure.

findings.item: SolidJS createMemo
findings.facts: Memos retain 'the results of a computation until its dependencies change' and are 'optimized to execute only once for each change in their dependencies.' A recomputed value that is strictly equal (===) does not trigger downstream updates. The page's examples use only signals, memos and effects with no JSX, but it does not explicitly say Solid's reactivity works standalone.
findings.use_for_engine: This confirms the same memo semantics. It gives no reason to add Solid; the runtime needs only the algorithm.

findings.item: TC39 Signals proposal
findings.facts: The README header says Stage 1. The status text mentions the April 2024 agenda and says the proposal 'can currently be thought of as "Stage 0".' API: Signal.State (get/set), Signal.Computed (get), and Signal.subtle (untrack, Watcher). The design is lazy, memoised, glitch-free and push-then-pull. A polyfill exists (proposal-signals/signal-polyfill), and the authors advise against relying on its stability. Design input came from maintainers of Angular, MobX, Preact, Solid, Svelte, Vue and others.
findings.use_for_engine: Shows broad agreement on the semantics. Do not depend on it: it is not standardised.

findings.item: alien-signals and the Vue 3.6 reactivity refactor
findings.facts: Described as 'The lightest signal library', using a push-pull algorithm. Its README lists influences: Vue 3 propagation, Preact's doubly linked lists, Svelte effect scheduling and Reactively's graph colouring. 'The core algorithm has been ported to v3.6' of Vue. The core avoids Array/Set/Map and recursion for performance. API: signal, computed, effect, effectScope, trigger, createReactiveSystem. npm on 2026-10-10: vue latest is 3.5.43, the rc tag is 3.6.0-rc.11, and alien-signals is 3.2.1. Bundlephobia reports @vue/reactivity 3.5.43 at 21.8 KB minified, 8.1 KB gzip.
findings.use_for_engine: If the owner wants to stay close to Vue, standalone @vue/reactivity works but is about 4x the size of signals-core. Since the frame engine is leaving Vue, prefer signals-core or a hand-written evaluator. Vue 3.6 is still a release candidate.

findings.item: tldraw signals (@tldraw/state)
findings.facts: Atoms take a debug name, an initial value and options: isEqual, historyLength (diffs kept for incremental updates) and computeDiff. Computeds are lazy ('they don't calculate until you call .get()') and cached. transact batches changes so effects run once; transaction adds rollback. react() and reactor() can schedule effects, for example with requestAnimationFrame. getDiffSince returns RESET_VALUE when the history is insufficient.
findings.use_for_engine: Two ideas to borrow: transaction-with-rollback for Lab drags, and rAF-scheduled effects for rendering. Incremental diffs are unnecessary at this scale.

findings.item: Observable runtime (define with explicit inputs)
findings.facts: variable.define(name, inputs, definition). A variable is 'only computed if any transitive output of the variable has an observer.' 'Circular inputs are not allowed; the variable will throw a ReferenceError upon evaluation.' If two variables share a name, both are overridden to throw. module.derive(specifiers, source) makes a copy with some variables replaced. License: ISC. Also covered in docs/research/06 #14.
findings.use_for_engine: This is the model for the document: every node lists its inputs by id. That makes dependencies serialisable, visible in the Lab and checkable for cycles at load time. derive maps to the frame variants.

findings.item: Theatre.js @theatre/dataverse
findings.facts: 'The reactive dataflow library' Theatre is built on, 'optimised for interactivity and animation.' Atoms hold state. Pointers are type-safe, referentially stable references to properties of atoms. Prisms derive values, recalculate when read while stale, and stay active only while subscribed. Tickers batch updates and align them to requestAnimationFrame.
findings.use_for_engine: Use pointer-style paths (for example 'medallion.arrows.station') as the stable address that handles, inspector rows and animation tracks bind to.

findings.item: Cassowary paper (Badros, Borning, Stuckey, ACM TOCHI 8(4) 2001, pp. 267-306)
findings.facts: I read the PDF text. Cassowary is an incremental solver for linear equalities and inequalities with constraint hierarchies (required vs preferred strengths). Dragging works by adding an edit constraint that is strongly preferred but not required, while weak stay constraints keep other points 'where they were unless there is some reason for them to move.' Efficient techniques exist if the network is acyclic. Most UI systems use one-way constraints or local propagation for acyclic multi-way constraints. Cycles need simultaneous solving. Cassowary is 'an order of magnitude' slower than local propagation (DeltaBlue) on re-solve, and the authors recommend 'a hybrid solver architecture' of cooperating subsolvers. 'Interaction times remain satisfactory for diagrams with 1000 constraints.' The authors also built CSVG, which extends SVG with constraints. The UW project page lists Apple's 2011 layout engine and Grid Style Sheets as users.
findings.use_for_engine: This is the primary-source answer to when a solver is needed. Use directed propagation for everything that has a direction. Use a simultaneous solver only for genuine cycles, as a separate subsolver. During drags, apply edit (strong) and stay (weak) semantics.

findings.item: kiwi.js / @lume/kiwi (Cassowary in TypeScript)
findings.facts: The original IjzerenHein/kiwi.js was archived on 2021-12-02 ('THIS REPOSITORY IS NO LONGER MAINTAINED') and points to lume/kiwi. @lume/kiwi is BSD-3-Clause, version 0.4.4, last npm change 2024-09-17. API: Solver, Variable, Expression, Constraint, Operator, Strength, addEditVariable, suggestValue, updateVariables. The project's own benchmark claims 10x faster creation and 2.3x faster solving than Cassowary.js, with no hardware details. Cassowary handles only linear constraints, so distances, tangency and curvature are out of reach.
findings.use_for_engine: Use it only if linear layout inequalities appear, such as 'medallion stays at least N px from the text column' or 'rail width at least X'. It cannot express any curve relationship. Likely unnecessary, because CSS and arithmetic nodes cover these cases.

findings.item: planegcs (FreeCAD Sketcher solver compiled to WASM)
findings.facts: npm @salusoft89/planegcs 1.3.0, last changed 2026-10-05. The LICENSE file is LGPL 2.1; package.json says LGPL-2.0-or-later. I inspected the tarball: planegcs.wasm is 484,003 bytes uncompressed. Primitives: point, line, circle, arc, ellipse, arc_of_ellipse, parabola, hyperbola (plus their arcs) and bspline. There is no clothoid or log-spiral primitive. constraints.ts defines 83 constraint types, including tangent_*, point_on_*, arc_length, equal_*, p2p_symmetric_*, proportional and point_on_bspline. Solvers: DogLeg (default), LevenbergMarquardt and BFGS, with SQP used when temporary constraints exist. The wrapper exposes dof(), get_conflicting(), get_redundant() and get_partially_redundant(). Wasm memory must be freed explicitly, and Vite needs a locateFile URL. The README notes that some constraints misbehave when set non-driving.
findings.use_for_engine: Lab-only and optional, for a design that truly needs mutual simultaneous constraints (for example tangent circles). It is useful for its DOF, conflict and redundancy diagnostics. Bake the results into parameters. Never ship it, and do not expect it to model the clothoid and log-spiral spines.

findings.item: SolveSpace solver library (slvs)
findings.facts: A sketch is made of parameters, entities and constraints. Entities and constraints are assigned to groups. 'A group is a set of entities and constraints that is solved simultaneously.' Constraints may reference entities in earlier groups, but 'only the entities within that group will be modified by the solver.' The initial guess 'determines which solution gets chosen' when several exist. There are three outcomes: OK; provably inconsistent, with failed[] listing the clashing constraints; or no solution found, with the unsatisfied constraints listed. slvs.h adds the dragged[] parameters, which the solver changes 'as little as possible'. Finding failed constraints costs 'about n times as long as just solving'. Entities are points, normals, distance, workplane, line segment, cubic, circle and arc of circle; there are no spirals.
