The library page says GPLv3. The npm package 'slvs' is an experimental WASM build: dist-tags latest 3.1.0-dev.14, stable 3.2.0, dev 3.3.0-dev.161, license 'GNU GPL V3'. A 2023 replicad issue says 'The API will probably change'.
findings.use_for_engine: Its group model matches the frame-engine design: a DAG of stages, each a small local solve, with upstream geometry fixed. Copy the 'dragged params change least' policy and the diagnostics vocabulary. Do not adopt the library: it is GPL, experimental in WASM and has no spirals.

findings.item: Penrose optimisation model
findings.facts: 'Under the hood, all constraint functions are implemented as energy functions.' A constraint's energy is greater than 0 if and only if it is violated. 'Penrose looks for a local minimum of the energy function by using numerical optimization.' API (docs/ref/api): compile(trio) -> PenroseState, optimize(state), step(state, {until}), isOptimized, toSVG. The trio has a 'variation' field that the page does not explain. Also covered in docs/research/05 #11.
findings.use_for_engine: Use energy minimisation only offline in the Lab, for 'encourage' goals such as even spacing or balanced density, and bake the result. A local minimum depends on the start point, so it is not a runtime tool.

findings.item: Clothoids library (Bertolazzi and Frego)
findings.facts: C++11 with a MATLAB mex interface. It implements 'G1 and G2 fitting with clothoids, spline of clothoids, circle arc and biarc.' Paper: Bertolazzi and Frego, 'G1 fitting with clothoids', Math. Methods Appl. Sci. 2015, doi:10.1002/mma.3114. It is not a JS library.
findings.use_for_engine: This is the kind of local, node-owned solve the engine needs. Example: a clothoid S-sweep from the medallion ring (heading and curvature given) to the stem (heading 90 degrees). The node solves it internally with Newton plus guard rails, and no global solver is involved. It would need a TS port or reimplementation from the paper.

findings.item: tldraw persistence and migrations
findings.facts: Snapshots are {document, session}. The document holds shapes, pages and bindings; the session holds camera, selection and UI. loadSnapshot replaces the document. 'When you load a snapshot from an older version, the store migrates it automatically.' createShapePropsMigrationIds gives ids that 'must start at 1 and increment', and each step has up() and down(). createMigrationSequence({sequenceId, sequence}) runs migrations at record, store or storage scope. 'Multiplayer sync uses the down migrations when a peer is running an older schema version.' The page does not say what happens with a newer-than-known snapshot.
findings.use_for_engine: Use an ordered migration list with integer ids, up() required and down() optional (single user). Split document and session: preview size, selection and zoom live in session state and are never written to the frame file.

findings.item: tldraw store
findings.facts: 'A record is a JSON object with an id and a typeName', with type-prefixed ids such as shape:, page: and binding:. The store 'validates all records against a schema' and checks the full record on every write. Scopes: document (persisted), session (local) and presence (synced, not persisted). Store.listen receives diffs: added, updated as [before, after], and removed.
findings.use_for_engine: Validate on every Lab write, not only on save, so a bad expression is caught at once. Use diffs to drive incremental recompute and the dirty indicator in the Lab.

findings.item: tldraw history (undo/redo)
findings.facts: The undo and redo stacks hold diffs and marks. 'Changes accumulate until you create a mark,' and are then flushed as one entry. markHistoryStoppingPoint is placed at the start of interactions. bail() and bailToMark() reverse changes 'without adding them to the redo stack', for example when a drag is cancelled. squashToMark merges everything since a mark into one step. editor.run history modes: record, record-preserveRedoStack and ignore. Remote changes are never recorded.
findings.use_for_engine: For a handle drag: mark on pointerdown, then live patches, then squash on pointerup (one undo step) or bail on Escape. Preview-only changes, such as scrubbing the contact-sheet size, use history:'ignore'.

findings.item: tldraw handles
findings.facts: ShapeUtil.getHandles(shape) returns handles in the shape's local coordinates. Fields: id, type (vertex, virtual, create, clone), index, x, y, optional snapType ('point' or 'align'), snapReferenceHandleId and label. onHandleDrag(shape, {handle, initial, isPrecise, isCreatingShape}) returns a partial shape, for example {props:{tailX, tailY}}. Lifecycle hooks: onHandleDragStart, onHandleDragEnd and onHandleDragCancel. Shift snaps to 15 degrees. getHandleSnapGeometry supplies snap outlines and points.
findings.use_for_engine: Each node type declares getHandles(resolvedNode) and onHandleDrag(...) -> parameter patch. Use the 'initial' snapshot to keep drags stable. Snap targets include stations on parent curves, golden ladder rungs and medallion anchor angles.

findings.item: tldraw bindings
findings.facts: A binding record holds fromId, toId and props. BindingUtil callbacks are onAfterChangeToShape/FromShape, onBeforeDeleteFromShape/ToShape, onBeforeDelete/onAfterDelete, and onBeforeIsolateFromShape/ToShape. The isolate callbacks let a binding 'bake in' its current state when the shapes are separated, so an arrow keeps its last endpoint. The editor keeps a per-shape binding index that updates incrementally.
findings.use_for_engine: Attachments (child at station s on a parent) are the frame engine's bindings. When the owner deletes or detaches a parent, offer 'bake': convert the dependent to absolute geometry instead of breaking it.

findings.item: Excalidraw file format and restore.ts (normalise-on-load migrations)
findings.facts: File: {type:'excalidraw', version, source, elements, appState, files} (docs.excalidraw.com json-schema). Element fields in packages/element/src/types.ts: seed ('so that the roughjs shape doesn't differ across renders'), version (incremented on each change), versionNonce, and index (a fractional index). restoreElementWithProperties fills defaults. It keeps unknown fields: 'spread the original element properties to not lose unknown ones for forward-compatibility'. It migrates legacy props (strokeSharpness to roundness, boundElementIds to boundElements) and deletes them. For old elements 'that would now use adaptive radius algo, use legacy algo instead' (ROUNDNESS.LEGACY). Binding schema v1 is detected and migrated to v2.
findings.use_for_engine: Three habits to copy. (1) Load tolerantly and keep unknown fields. (2) Make the algorithm version part of the data: node.algo:'v1'. When the clothoid fit or tile-fitting maths improves, committed frames keep their exact look until the owner opts in. (3) Stable seeds if any jitter is ever used.

findings.item: Figma multiplayer document model and undo rule
findings.facts: 'Every Figma document is a tree of objects, similar to the HTML DOM', best pictured as 'Map<ObjectID, Map<Property, Value>>'. A conflict happens only when two clients change the same property on the same object. The parent link is stored as a property on the child, together with a fractional-index position, as one atomic property. Figma rejected OT as 'unnecessarily complex' and uses CRDT-inspired, server-authoritative merging. Undo rule: if you undo a lot, copy something, and redo back to the present, 'the document should not change.'
findings.use_for_engine: Use a flat node map keyed by id, with properties as the unit of change and relationships stored on the child. This also gives clean, property-sized git diffs. The undo rule is a good acceptance test for the Lab's history.

findings.item: Immer patches
findings.facts: Enable with enablePatches(). produceWithPatches returns [nextState, patches, inversePatches]. applyPatches replays them. Each patch has op (replace, add, remove), path (an array, unlike RFC 6902 strings) and value. The docs list it as a 'basis for undo/redo'. 'Immer does not guarantee the generated set of patches will be optimal.'
findings.use_for_engine: Lab history entries are {label, patches, inversePatches}. Patches on a JSON document are also readable in a history panel. Coalesce many pointermove patches into one squashed entry.

findings.item: Command pattern for undo (Nystrom, Game Programming Patterns)
findings.facts: An undo() method 'reverses the game state changed by the corresponding execute() method'. The command must remember the previous state itself. Keep 'a list of commands and a reference to the current one'. A new command after undoing discards the commands after current. Redo advances the pointer and re-executes. Persistent data structures are the alternative: undo switches back to the old object, which is 'much cheaper than cloning the entire object'.
findings.use_for_engine: Named commands (setParam, attach, bake, addVariant, importMotif) give human-readable history labels. Immutable document plus patches is the persistent-structure variant, which fits a JSON document best.

findings.item: Theatre.js core/studio split
findings.facts: README: @theatre/core is Apache-2.0 and @theatre/studio is AGPL-3.0. 'Your project's final bundle only includes @theatre/core'. Projects manual: the tweaks and animations are 'the project's state'. While the Studio is open, state lives in localStorage and is exported as a JSON file, then loaded with getProject('My Project', {state: projectState}). The 0.5 docs (theatrejs.com/docs/0.5/getting-started/with-three-js) say to remove studio.initialize/extend for deploy, or gate them with if (import.meta.env.DEV) and rely on tree-shaking. Core API: sequence.play({iterationCount, range, rate, direction, rafDriver}) returns a Promise that resolves true on completion and false if interrupted. types.number range is 'just a visual guide, not a validation rule'. Status: 'Theatre.js 1.0 is around the corner', and 'We have temporarily moved development to a private repo'. Last npm publish of core and studio: 0.7.2 on 2024-05-19.
findings.use_for_engine: Mirror the split exactly: frame-core plus the JSON document ships; frame-lab never does. Unlike Theatre, save to real files rather than localStorage. Theatre's play() API is a good shape for the later tab-change animations. Use Theatre as a reference, not a dependency, because public development is stalled.

findings.item: Rive .riv format versioning, runtimes and N-slicing
findings.facts: The file starts with the 'RIVE' fingerprint, then major and minor versions (varuint), a file ID and a table of contents of property keys with 2-bit backing types. A runtime that does not know a key can read past it. 'Runtimes are compatible with only a single major Rive export format version'. Minor versions are compatible, and 'Unsupported features are treated as no-ops.' Objects are a flat ordered list; parents are referenced by index. Official runtimes are open source under MIT (rive.app/docs/runtimes/getting-started). N-Slicing (rive.app/docs/editor/layouts/n-slicing) generalises 9-slice: axes split artwork into segments that alternate between fixed and scaling, and scaling segments can stretch or repeat (repeat only for raster).
findings.use_for_engine: Versioning rule for the runtime: refuse an unknown major, and treat unknown minor additions as optional and ignorable. The editor stays private while the runtime is small and separate. Fixed and scaling segments are the minimal vocabulary for frame edges; the engine goes further with whole-tile refits along spines.

findings.item: Graphite editor architecture
findings.facts: The frontend (TypeScript and Svelte) is meant to be 'as lightweight and minimal as possible'. The editor core is Rust compiled to WebAssembly and is where 'business logic occurs'. A thin wrapper exposes its message system to TS. 'At its heart is the message system', with backend-to-frontend messages queued to a dispatcher. Graphene is the node-graph engine that 'manages and renders the documents'; 'Graphene programs are compiled while being edited live by the user.' docs/research/06 #10 covers canvas and graph as two views of one document, and hand-override nodes.
findings.use_for_engine: Keep the Lab UI a thin shell over the same evaluator the site uses, and route all edits through one command or message channel. The graph view and the canvas are two views of one document.

findings.item: Cuttle parameters
findings.facts: Parameters define a value 'in one place' and are referenced throughout. Parameters can reference other parameters and use math expressions. Expressions can be multi-line JavaScript that returns any value, including arrays, objects or functions. Project parameters are global. Component parameters are local, and each instance can override them. docs/research/06 #8 covers extract-to-parameter and forkable modifiers.
findings.use_for_engine: Use two parameter scopes: frame-wide (ink weight, golden steps) and per-motif-master, with per-instance overrides (four mirrored corner medallions). Unlike Cuttle, keep the expression language arithmetic-only so documents stay safe and readable.

findings.item: Zod 4 to JSON Schema
findings.facts: z.toJSONSchema() targets draft-2020-12 by default, with draft-07, draft-04 and openapi-3.0 also available. z.fromJSONSchema() is 'experimental'. .meta() and registries emit interlinked schemas with $ref. Unrepresentable types (date, map, set, transform, bigint and others) throw by default. Bundlephobia reports zod 4.6.5 at 385 KB minified, 88.6 KB gzip for the full package entry.
findings.use_for_engine: Write the document types once in Zod (Lab, CI and Node tools). Generate frame.schema.json so a $schema line gives VS Code autocomplete and validation while the owner hand-edits. Keep Zod out of the shipped runtime.

findings.item: RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme
findings.facts: Recursively sorts object keys by UTF-16 code units, serialises numbers per ECMAScript (NaN and Infinity are errors), and forbids whitespace ('Whitespace between JSON tokens MUST NOT be emitted'). Its purpose is hashing and signing. It is Informational, not standards track.
findings.use_for_engine: Use JCS for content hashes (cache keys, snapshot ids). For the committed file, use the same ordering and number rules but pretty-print, because JCS's single line gives useless git diffs.

findings.item: Godot TSCN text scene format
findings.facts: TSCN files are 'mostly human-readable and easy for version control systems to manage'. The header declares the format version (format=3 for Godot 4, 2 for Godot 3). Fixed section order: descriptor, external resources, internal resources, nodes, connections. String ids reference resources. uid and unique_id let files and nodes be tracked through moves and renames.
findings.use_for_engine: A precedent for a deliberately VCS-friendly editor format. Use a fixed section order (header, params, motifs, nodes, variants, animations), string ids and an explicit format version.

findings.item: Fractional indexing (rocicorp)
findings.facts: generateKeyBetween(a, b) returns a base-62 string key that sorts between two keys, so items can be inserted without renumbering. It is based on David Greenspan's 'Implementing Fractional Indexing' and used for ordered sequences in realtime editing. Excalidraw's element.index uses it.
findings.use_for_engine: Probably unnecessary for a single-user file. Use explicit layer numbers or arrays for paint order. Adopt fractional keys only if inserts start causing large renumbering diffs.

findings.item: math.js expression security
findings.facts: 'Mathjs versions 4 and newer does not use JavaScript's eval under the hood'. The parser 'actively prevents access to JavaScripts internal eval and new Function'. The docs still warn 'there are unknown security vulnerabilities' are possible and suggest Web Workers for untrusted input.
findings.use_for_engine: Relationship expressions in the document should use a tiny hand-written parser to an AST: arithmetic, param refs, phi, sqrt, ln, trig, min, max, clamp, lerp and rung. No eval or new Function, so a strict CSP stays possible. math.js is unnecessary weight for this.

findings.item: Vite plugin API and multi-page builds
findings.facts: configureServer is mostly used for 'adding custom middlewares'. apply: 'serve' or 'build' (or a function) restricts a plugin to dev or build. Client to server: import.meta.hot.send. Server: server.ws.on and server.ws.send, with event names to be prefixed. Build guide: multi-page apps list several .html files as inputs. The current docs use build.rolldownOptions; this repo is on Vite 7 (package.json ^7.0.6), so check which key it expects. build.lib produces a distributable library.
findings.use_for_engine: Run the Lab as lab.html served only in dev, plus a plugin with apply:'serve' whose middleware validates and writes frames/*.frame.json to disk. Saves are real files that git sees, and the blog tab picks them up through the dev server. build.lib can later package frame-core on its own.

findings.item: Floating-point determinism of JS Math
findings.facts: 'Many Math functions have a precision that's implementation-dependent. This means that different browsers can give a different result. Even the same JavaScript engine on a different OS or architecture can give different results!'
findings.use_for_engine: Deterministic output means rounding on serialisation (SVG coordinates and the document), snapshot tests in one engine (Node in CI) with a tolerance compare, and never using raw float equality to decide whether art changed.

findings.item: prefers-reduced-motion
findings.facts: Detects a user setting 'to minimize the amount of non-essential motion'. Values are no-preference and reduce. Animations 'can trigger discomfort for those with vestibular motion disorders'.
findings.use_for_engine: Every animation entry in the document declares its reduced-motion behaviour (skip or jump to end). The runtime reads matchMedia once and on change.

findings.item: Existing repo code (local evidence)
findings.facts: CornerOrnament already carries '// Backward-compat fallback fields' (strokeWidth, dash). That is an informal migration living in the type. src/ornaments/hand-drawn.json pretty-prints every [x, y] pair over 4 lines, which makes diffs noisy. The uncommitted framing/ spike already has pure helpers that map onto node types: rung(base, step), fitRepeats(length, period, step), weave(...) with over/under pieces, and rosette(...).
findings.use_for_engine: Replace fallback fields with explicit migrations. Write numeric tuples on one line. Promote the spike's pure functions to frame-core operators (repeatFit, goldenRung, weave, rosette) behind typed node definitions.

gaps.recommendation:
ONE DOCUMENT, TWO PROGRAMS: frame-core runs the frame on the site; frame-lab edits it and never ships (the Theatre.js core/studio split).

1. SHARED DOCUMENT: frames/<name>.frame.json, committed to git, the single source of truth.
- Header: {"$schema":"./frame.schema.json", "format":"parkington-frame", "formatVersion":1}. The JSON Schema is generated from Zod types (z.toJSONSchema, draft 2020-12), so hand edits in VS Code are validated.
- params: named design values {value | expr, unit, range, frozen?, scope: frame | motif}. Golden constants are frozen expressions (phi, flame.b = ln(phi)/(pi/2)), so no drag can break them. Ratio choices are explicit dials (spacing law uniform | geometric(r); spiral b golden | free), as the 07 analysis requires.
- nodes: a flat map keyed by stable, readable ids. This is Figma's Map<ObjectID, Map<Property, Value>> with the relationship stored on the child. Each node is {type, inputs:{role: nodeId}, args:{literal | param ref | expr}, algo?:"v1", meta?:{Lab-only notes, lock, colour}}. Example: "flame.leaves": {type:"copyAlong", inputs:{proto:"leaf.master", spine:"flame.tipSpiral"}, args:{stations:{law:"equalAngle", step:"flame.step", count:6}, scale:"radiusOnSpine", rotate:"tangent + 12deg"}}.
- A closed, typed relation vocabulary, not free JavaScript:
  - anchors: pageBox, inset, corner, rail
  - curves: line, arc, clothoid, logSpiral, eulerSpline, importedPath
  - attach: child at station s on parent, side and offset, continuity G0/G1/G2
  - copies: copyAlong, similarity/gnomon about a pole, mirror, repeatFit with whole tiles
  - families: offsets of one spine, or interpolation between two guides, with a spacing law
  - weave: over/under derived from crossing parity
  - assert: minGap, noCrossing, offset < radius, goldenPitch within tolerance, tiles >= 1
  These formalise the copy, scale, mirror and attach operations the 07 analysis found in the drawing.
- Expressions: a tiny arithmetic language parsed to an AST by a hand-written parser. No eval or new Function, so the site keeps a strict CSP.
- Thresholds: variants:[{id, when: predicate on derived room measures (rail.width, page.width, aspect), overrides:{param: value}, swap:{nodeId: altNode}}], first match wins. Add a hysteresis margin so a resize near a boundary does not flicker. Inside a variant, scale continuously between two designed endpoints (the Utopia pattern, docs/research/05). Example ladder: 3-strand plait, then 2-ribbon twist, then a plain double rule.
- animations: [{id, trigger:"route-change" | "load", target:"medallion.arrows.station", from, to, duration, easing, reducedMotion:"skip" | "end"}]. The arrows are attachments at station s on a ribbon spine, so 'running down the track' means animating s. The weave node exposes isOver(strand, s), so a moving arrow passes under crossings correctly.
- Deterministic writer:
  - fixed key order per schema, and the node map sorted by id
  - numbers rounded (about 3-4 decimals for drawing units, 6 for ratios)
  - [x, y] tuples kept on one line, 2-space indent, trailing newline
  - JCS (RFC 8785) only for hashes and cache keys; it strips whitespace, so it does not suit git diffs
- Versioning:
  - integer formatVersion with an ordered migration list (tldraw style: ids from 1; up() required, down() optional), and one fixture file per old version tested in CI
  - load tolerantly and keep unknown fields (Excalidraw restore.ts)
  - the runtime refuses a newer major and ignores optional unknowns (the Rive rule)
  - when an algorithm's output changes, keep the old one addressable through node.algo (Excalidraw keeps ROUNDNESS.LEGACY for old elements), so committed art never shifts silently
  - replace frameSettings.ts's 'Backward-compat fallback fields' with real migrations

2. RUNTIME (frame-core, shipped): pure TypeScript, no Vue, no solver, no Zod.
- evaluate(doc, ctx {width, height, route, time, reducedMotion}) -> Scene, then an SVG emitter (filled outlines for variable width, per docs/research/04-05).
- Explicit DAG: inputs and param refs give the edges. Sort topologically once at load; a cycle is an error that names the loop (Observable throws on circular inputs).
- Incremental and lazy: a version-stamped memo per node, using the Preact 'Signal Boosting' algorithm. Either hand-write about 150 lines, or wrap each node in a @preact/signals-core computed (about 2 KB gzip). Use epsilon or structural equality on geometry so unchanged outputs stop propagation. Nodes of inactive variants never run.
- Curve kernel:
  - arc-length lookup tables, plus tangent and curvature queries
  - analytic clothoid, log-spiral and Euler-spline evaluation
  - safe offset families
  - cubic Bézier fitting at a tolerance for SVG output
  - local, node-owned solves only (for example G2 clothoid Hermite fits, Bertolazzi-Frego style): warm-started, with iteration caps, a NaN check and a fallback to the last good value
  - no Math.random; seeded PRNG only
- Drivers: ResizeObserver feeds ctx. A route change fires triggers. A requestAnimationFrame loop runs only while an animation plays, and it re-evaluates only that animation's dependents. Moving parts render as their own SVG groups with stable ids.

3. FRAME LAB (frame-lab, dev only)
- Serving: lab.html is served only by the Vite dev server. A plugin with apply:'serve' adds a configureServer middleware that validates and then writes frames/*.frame.json (real files git sees; no localStorage-only state). The blog in another tab reloads from the same JSON. The Lab uses the same frame-core evaluator.
- Panels:
  - named-parameter inspector with ranges, golden-ladder steps and frozen locks
  - canvas with a construction overlay (spines, poles, stations, curvature combs)
  - contact sheet of viewport sizes, with variant boundaries marked
  - validators/asserts panel (golden pitch, minimum printable gap, crossings, offset vs radius)
  - read-only dependency-graph view
  - Illustrator import that fits a curve family, reports residuals and snaps only on request (docs/research/06-07)
- Handles: declared per node type, like tldraw's getHandles/onHandleDrag. Each handle names the 1-2 params it may change. A drag solves argmin |handle(params) - mouse|^2 over those params only (edit), holding the rest (stay). This follows Cassowary edit/stay and SolveSpace's dragged params. Snap targets: stations, rungs and anchor angles. Reject NaN or high-error steps (the Recursive Drawing guard rails).
- Undo and history:
  - the document is immutable; commands produce immer patches and inverse patches
  - pointerdown sets a mark; pointerup squashes the drag into one step; Escape bails (tldraw)
  - session state (selection, zoom, preview size) is kept apart and never undone
  - git commits are the long-term history
  - deleting a parent offers 'bake to absolute geometry' (tldraw isolate)
- Solver policy:
  - use the DAG by default
  - use a global simultaneous solve only for a genuine cycle the owner wants (for example mutual tangency): run planegcs in the Lab for DOF and conflict/redundancy reports, bake the numbers into params, and keep the relation as an assert so drift is flagged
  - add kiwi/Cassowary only if linear layout inequalities appear
  - run Penrose-style optimisation (spacing, balance) offline, then bake

4. BUILD ORDER
1. Schema v1, the evaluator and the SVG emitter, plus a Node CLI that renders a document at a bracket of sizes for snapshot tests. Snapshots run in one engine with tolerance, because Math precision differs between browsers.
2. Lab v0: parameter panel, live preview, contact sheet, file save, undo.
3. Handles and validators.
4. Variants and thresholds.
5. Illustrator fit/import, plus optional planegcs.
6. Animations, then a small timeline UI.
cautions: Do not build a general constraint solver as the core. The browser-ready CAD solvers (planegcs, SolveSpace) have no clothoid or log-spiral primitives. Cassowary/kiwi handle only linear constraints. Numerical drag solvers can jump to a different solution (Apparatus, in docs/research/06). The SolveSpace docs say the initial guess decides which solution is chosen.

Licences and maturity: planegcs is LGPL-2.1 (its package.json says LGPL-2.0-or-later) with a 484 KB wasm. SolveSpace is GPLv3, and its npm 'slvs' WASM build is experimental (the latest dist-tag points to an old 3.1.0-dev.14). kiwi.js was archived in 2021, and @lume/kiwi was last published in 2024-09. Theatre.js moved development to a private repo and last published 0.7.2 on npm in 2024-05. Use it as a design reference, not a dependency.

Standards in flux: TC39 Signals is Stage 1 at most (its README also says to treat it as 'Stage 0'). Vue 3.6's alien-signals reactivity is still a release candidate (3.6.0-rc.11; stable is 3.5.43 as of 2026-10-10).

Bundle weight: the full Zod 4.6.5 entry is about 88.6 KB gzip according to bundlephobia. Keep validation in the Lab, CI and Node tools, not in the shipped runtime. Bundlephobia rate-limited me before I could get sizes for alien-signals, immer or @lume/kiwi, so I give no figures for them.

Determinism: JS Math precision is implementation-dependent across browsers and operating systems (MDN). Round serialised numbers, compare SVG snapshots with a tolerance in one engine, and never use float equality to decide that the art changed.

Committed art can shift silently when the engine's maths improves. Pin the algorithm per node (node.algo), as Excalidraw does with ROUNDNESS.LEGACY, and require a migration plus a fixture test for every schema change.

Keep the document hand-readable and the relation vocabulary small and closed. The research record warns about unreadable generated equations (Sketch-n-Sketch), spaghetti graphs (Davis: 97.5% of 2,002 Grasshopper models had no modules) and too many sliders (Prototypo/METAFONT). The owner is a designer, not a full-time programmer.
Never use eval or new Function for relationship expressions. Even math.js, which avoids eval, warns of possible unknown vulnerabilities. A hand-written arithmetic parser keeps a strict CSP.
Theatre-style localStorage state can be lost. The Lab must write real files through a dev-only middleware, and must not hold hidden state that is missing from the JSON.

Several details come from documentation summaries rather than full source reads: the tldraw behaviour for snapshots newer than the schema (unstated), Penrose's 'variation' semantics (unexplained on the API page), Theatre's exact tree-shaking guarantee (the docs rely on the bundler; a dynamic import of studio is safer), and whether Vite 7 in this repo uses rollupOptions or rolldownOptions for multi-page inputs. Verify these when implementing.

The FreeCAD wiki (for Sketcher DOF and redundancy wording) was blocked by bot protection. The planegcs diagnostics claims come from its TypeScript wrapper source (get_conflicting, get_redundant, dof), not from FreeCAD documentation.

gaps.summary:
Practical TypeScript curve kernel for the frame engine. I read primary sources: Levien's blog posts, the kurbo source, libspiro, spiro-js, Levien's own JS research code, Bertolazzi and Frego, the Cephes Fresnel code via stdlib, the log-aesthetic curve (LAC) paper, Wikipedia geometry pages, npm metadata and Iosevka's source. I also ran scratch measurements on the curve sizes from 07-drawing-analysis.md.

1. Define every curve family intrinsically, as tangent angle theta(s) and curvature kappa(s) over its own arc length. Arc length then comes for free, G2 at a join is a simple comparison of (x, y, theta, kappa), and one evaluator covers line, arc, clothoid, log spiral and LAC.
2. Clothoids do not need Fresnel integrals. Composite 16-point Gauss-Legendre is accurate to about 1e-9 of the length on a single piece that turns pi radians, and about 1e-13 with two pieces. It needs no special case when kappa1 = 0, at inflections or near circles, which is exactly where the Fresnel completing-the-square form loses precision. Log spirals have closed forms and need no quadrature.
3. For knot-drawn dominant sweeps, the npm package `spiro` (be5invis/spiro-js) is the realistic choice. It is Apache-2.0 or MIT, written in TypeScript, and the Iosevka typeface depends on it. It has two traps. It returns no convergence status. Its default Bezier output (subdivide to 1 rad of bend, arms = L/3) is off by about 0.26% of the radius, roughly 0.2u on the medallion ring.
4. Converting to Bezier is cheap if handles are chosen well. Arms = L/3 is 50 to 9000 times worse than the arc-correct rule. With equal-turn subdivision and arms = chord/(3cos^2(dtheta/4)), I measured 2-3 cubics for the 54-degree clothoid limb, 2-3 for the 170-degree ring, 6-8 per golden-spiral turn and 10-13 for a 2.5-turn volute, at 0.05u to 0.01u. The gold standard is kurbo's area-and-moment quartic fit (O(n^6)), which has no npm or WASM build. Port fit.rs and its solvers (Apache-2.0 or MIT) later.
5. Avoid cusps by construction: an offset d needs |d| < R_min on the concave side. Offset arc length is L + d*dtheta. Weave strands need A < R_min of the spine and a ribbon half-width h < lambda^2/(4 pi^2 A). Nested lines around spiral eyes should be rotated copies of the spiral about its pole, which never cross and space geometrically, not parallel offsets. Variable-width outlines are p ± w(s)n with w*kappa < 1. Fill them nonzero, as Levien and Uguray do. Do not use perfect-freehand for exact work.
6. Hobby is a preview and fallback only. Superellipses (Knuth's 8-knot construction, superness s = 2^(-1/n)) suit cartouche and jewel outlines and join straight sides with G2. Two-point G1 clothoids come from Bertolazzi and Frego's Newton method (at most 5 iterations). G2 two-point data needs 3 clothoids.

findings.item: Euler-spiral/clothoid evaluation: Levien's polynomial integrator (JS, Apache-2.0/MIT) and libspiro's version
findings.facts: Levien's spline-research/spiro.js (header: Copyright 2018 Raph Levien, Apache-2.0 or MIT) has integ_spiro(k0,k1,k2,k3), commented 'tuned to give an accuracy within 1e-9'. It uses a single order-12 Taylor expansion when 0.2*k0^2 + |k1| < 1, otherwise the same expansion over 4 sub-intervals. The curve is normalised to arc length 1 over [-0.5, 0.5], with k0 = total turning and k1 = curvature slope. libspiro (FontForge fork, GPL-3.0-or-later) uses ORDER 12 and N_IS 4 in integrate_spiro. spiro-js's integrate_spiro is the same order-12, N=4 code. All three avoid Fresnel functions entirely.
findings.use_for_engine: Optional fast path for clothoid points: port integ_spiro (about 100 lines, permissive licence) from Levien's repo, not from GPL libspiro. Use it in a chord-normalised frame, with subdivision when the turning is large.

findings.item: Fresnel integrals (Cephes via @stdlib) and why completing the square is fragile
findings.facts: @stdlib/math-base-special-fresnel 0.3.1 (Apache-2.0, published 2026-02-08) is a port of Cephes fresnl. It uses rational power series for x^2 < 2.5625, auxiliary f/g asymptotic rational functions above that, and returns 0.5 for |x| > 36974. The stated relative error on [0,10] over 10,000 trials is peak 2.0e-15 for S and 1.8e-15 for C (rms 3.2e-16 and 3.3e-16). Bertolazzi and Frego (arXiv 1305.6644) say the generalised Fresnel integrals X_k(a,b), Y_k(a,b) are 'inaccurate when |a| is small' because z appears in denominators. They switch to series below a threshold: for |a| < 1e-4 with p=2 the error is below 6.26e-18, and with p=3 below 1.6e-26. The (a,b) form used in their paper is the clothoid's own quadratic angle function, so a small a is the near-straight or near-circle case.
findings.use_for_engine: Do not make standard Fresnel C/S the main clothoid evaluator: the medallion limbs pass through kappa1 ≈ 0 regions and inflections. If closed-form Fresnel is ever wanted, use the Cephes rational approximations with a small-|a| series fallback.

findings.item: Measured: composite Gauss-Legendre quadrature as the universal intrinsic-curve evaluator (my scratch test)
findings.facts: Integrating (cos theta(s), sin theta(s)) against a 20,000-piece reference, on unit length. Clothoid turning pi rad (kappa 0 to 2pi): 16-point GL on 1 piece gives error 1.4e-9; 2 pieces 7.5e-14; the 8-point rule needs 4 pieces for 1.2e-8. S-clothoid with kappa -6..6: 16-point gives 1.5e-8 on 1 piece and 1.3e-12 on 2. Golden log spiral over 2 turns with uniform pieces converges slowly because of the pole-side growth: 16-point with 8 pieces gives 1.6e-6. Script: (local scratch file)
findings.use_for_engine: One evaluator for clothoids and LACs: composite 16-point Gauss-Legendre on sub-pieces each turning at most pi/2, with cumulative positions cached per piece. It needs no branch for kappa1 = 0, kappa = 0 or inflections. Log spirals use closed forms instead.

findings.item: G1 clothoid between two posed points: Bertolazzi and Frego (arXiv 1305.6644; Clothoids C++ library, BSD-2-Clause)
findings.facts: The method reduces the 3-equation system to the zero of one function g(A) = Y(2A, delta - A, phi0). The paper proves an interval where the zero exists and is unique. The simple guess is A ≈ 3(phi0 + phi1); better least-squares guesses (20a/20b) are tabulated. Table I buildClothoid is about 8 lines. On a 1024x1024 grid of angles with tolerance 1e-10, guess (19) took at most 5 Newton iterations (63% took 4), and guess (20b) took 3 iterations in 96.6% of cases. The reference implementation is github.com/ebertolazzi/Clothoids (C++, BSD 2-clause licence text, pushed 2026-10-01), which also offers G2 clothoid splines, biarcs, point-clothoid distance and intersections. Their JCAM 2018 paper proves that G2 Hermite data cannot always be met by one clothoid, nor by two. The general scheme uses three arcs (8 equations in 10 unknowns, reduced to 2), and in their tests it always converged within 5 Newton iterations.
findings.use_for_engine: Port buildClothoid (Newton plus guess (20b)) for one-clothoid G1 connectors, such as stem to anchor with fixed tangents, evaluating X and Y with the Gauss-Legendre integrator instead of Fresnel moments. Use 3-clothoid G2 Hermite (https://iris.unitn.it/handle/11572/210452) only when an exact curvature hand-off at both ends is required.

findings.item: Levien's JS fit_euler / EulerSegment (G1 Euler spiral from end angles)
findings.facts: In spline-research/spiro.js, fit_euler(th0, th1) finds k0 and k1 of an Euler spiral whose chord is (0,0)-(1,0) with the given end tangent angles. It runs a secant iteration for at most 10 steps to |error| < 1e-9 and throws 'fit_euler diverges' otherwise. EulerSegment exposes th(t), xy(t) and kEndpoints() (end curvatures scaled by the chord). The repo was relicensed from GPL to Apache-2.0 and MIT in May 2019 (Levien, 'An update on spline licensing'). It is research code, last pushed in 2020.
findings.use_for_engine: A permissively licensed, compact alternative to Bertolazzi-Frego for G1 clothoid segments in a chord-normalised frame. Catch the throw and fall back to an arc or Hobby piece.

findings.item: Spiro (Euler-spiral G2 splines through on-curve knots) in TS: npm `spiro` (be5invis/spiro-js)
findings.facts: Version 3.0.1, published 2024-04-02, Apache-2.0 OR MIT, written in TypeScript, 43 KB unpacked, depends only on tslib. Point types are 'corner' | 'open' | 'open_end' | 'left' | 'right' | 'g2' | 'g4'. The API includes spiroToBezier, spiroToBezierOnContext and spiroToArcsOnContext, the last returning SpiroArc objects with eval/derivative. Iosevka's @iosevka/geometry depends on 'spiro': '^3.0.1'. Source details that matter: solve_spiro loops at most 10 Newton iterations, breaks at norm < 1e-12, and always returns 0, so no convergence flag reaches the caller. Bezier output uniformly subdivides each arc until every part has bend ≤ delta (default 1 rad, up to 32 parts), then uses arms = derivative/3. By comparison, libspiro (GPL-3.0) iterates up to 60 times, reports convergence and uses the same arm rule. Levien lists Spiro's real failure modes ('A new spline', 2018): non-unique solutions, failure to converge with 'wild patterns', loop reversal at cusps, and confusing one-way constraints.
findings.use_for_engine: Use for knot-drawn dominant curves: medallion S-sweeps, ribbon centrelines. Prefer spiroToArcsOnContext and feed the arcs to the engine's own fitter, or pass delta ≈ 0.25 rad. Wrap every solve with a residual or sanity check (NaN, bend > pi, end-tangent mismatch) and fall back to Hobby or the last good solution while dragging.

findings.item: Iosevka's spiro-based stroke expansion (a shipped precedent)
findings.facts: @iosevka/geometry/src/spiro-expand.mjs builds a BiKnot per centreline knot with left and right widths d1 and d2. expand() places lhs = knot + d1·normal and rhs = knot - d2·normal using the knot's tangent normal (with a contrast factor). iterateNormals() re-solves Spiro through the midpoints of the lhs and rhs points to refine the normals. 'Unimportant' knots are interpolated. The package also exports spiro-pen-expand. Iosevka is a whole typeface generated this way in JS.
findings.use_for_engine: A cheap way to turn a spine into variable-width outlines: offset the knots, not the curve, and re-solve. Good for ribbons and leaf blades with smooth widths. It is approximate and has no cusp handling, so keep width < radius of curvature.

findings.item: Measured: cubic handle rule for arcs; why arms = L/3 (Spiro's default) is a trap
findings.facts: Maximum radial error per unit radius, arms = L/3 versus arms = (4/3)tan(theta/4): 90° 1.52e-2 vs 2.73e-4; 57.3° (1 rad) 2.56e-3 vs 1.81e-5; 28.6° 1.62e-4 vs 2.83e-7; 14.3° 1.02e-5 vs 4.42e-9. Arms = L/3 converges as O(theta^4); the tangent rule as O(theta^6). At Spiro's default 1 rad bend on the medallion ring (R ≈ 86u) the L/3 rule errs by about 0.22u, comparable to the 0.5-1u stroke width. Mortensen reports that a minimax-optimised quarter circle is 'five times better' than the standard constant; the page's constants could not be extracted as text. The general form of the tangent rule is arm = chord/(3cos^2(dtheta/4)), which is exact for circles. Script: .../scratchpad/exp/arcerr.mjs
findings.use_for_engine: Emit exact circles with the SVG A command. Inside fitted outlines, use 4/3·tan(dtheta/4)·R with dtheta ≤ 60-90°. Never use derivative/3 handles on bends larger than about 0.25 rad.

findings.item: Measured: how many cubics each ornament family needs (sizes from 07-drawing-analysis)
findings.facts: Counts at tolerances 0.05u / 0.01u. Ring arc (170°, R 85.8): L/3 arms 5/7; best G1 arms 2/3; arc-rule with equal-turn pieces 2/3. Clothoid limb (135u, kappa 0 to 0.0139, 54°): 3/4; 2/3; 2/3. Golden spiral (1 turn, r ≤ 45, 131.2u long): L/3 with equal-length pieces 13/20 and with equal-turn pieces 8/11; best arms (equal length) 5/8; arc-rule (equal turn) 6/8. Volute (b = 0.15, 2.5 turns, r ≤ 20): L/3 32/50 or 16/24; best 15/20; arc-rule 10/13. Single-segment error on the clothoid limb, whole limb: L/3 0.584u vs best arms 0.0745u. Verified separately that 1 golden turn ending at r = 45 gives chord 38.4346 = 45(1 - phi^-4), with growth per turn 6.8541 = phi^4 and pitch 17.0324°. These come from a crude grid optimiser and sampled maximum distance, so treat them as order-of-magnitude. Scripts: .../scratchpad/exp/fitexp.mjs, fitexp2.mjs, chk.mjs
findings.use_for_engine: SVG output stays tiny: tens of cubics per stroke. Equal-turn subdivision matters for spirals, and the handle rule matters more than the count. A phase-1 fitter (equal-turn split, arc-corrected arms, sampled error check) is good enough before porting kurbo.

findings.item: Cubic Bezier fitting with error bounds: Levien 2021 + kurbo fit.rs (Apache-2.0 OR MIT)
findings.facts: Method: G1 fit with fixed endpoints and end tangents. The two arm lengths are chosen so the signed area, (3/20)(2d0 sin th0 + 2d1 sin th1 - d0 d1 sin(th0+th1)), and the x-moment match the source. This reduces to a quartic. The error is O(n^6): halving cuts error 64x. C-shaped sources usually give 3 similar candidates, and the 4th root is a looping 'nemesis' to exclude. kurbo's ParamCurveFit trait has three methods: sample_pt_tangent(t, sign), sample_pt_deriv(t), and break_cusp(range). Moments come from 16-point Gauss-Legendre with Green's theorem. Error is estimated from N_SAMPLE = 20 samples as an approximation to the Fréchet distance, with an arc-length mode for 'spicy' curves; the docs say this is not a rigorous guarantee. fit_to_bezpath halves adaptively, giving about 1.5x the optimal count. fit_to_bezpath_opt is near-optimal and about 50x slower. A long-arm 'bump' penalty applies (elbow 0.65, slope 2.0), and try_fit_line handles tiny chords and cusps. kurbo 0.13.1, repo pushed 2026-10-08. I found no official npm or WASM build. Simplification example (Levien 2023): tolerance 0.15 gives 44 segments, 0.05 gives 60 and 0.01 gives 90.
findings.use_for_engine: Phase 2: port fit.rs plus common.rs (solve_quartic per Orellana-De Michele, solve_cubic, solve_quadratic, ITP, Gauss-Legendre tables) to TS behind a Fittable {sample(t) → point and derivative; cusp?(range)} interface. Use it for all analytic families, offsets, weaves and outlines, and to simplify imported Illustrator paths. Blog: https://raphlinus.github.io/curves/2021/03/11/bezier-fitting.html

findings.item: Parallel curves (offsets) and cusps: Levien 2022, Wikipedia Parallel curve
findings.facts: The exact offset of a cubic Bezier is an algebraic curve of degree 10, and offsets of a degree-n Bezier have degree 4n-2. Offset curvature is k_d = k/(1 + dk), so R_d = R + d, and cusps appear where the distance equals the radius of curvature. Levien's offset fit uses area/moment plus a quartic and is O(n^6). The O(n^6) area/moment fit runs in about 12 µs per segment in JS (M1 Max, Chrome). Tiller-Hanson is only O(n^2), an earlier Euler-spiral method O(n^4) and shape control O(n^5). One cubic can have four cusps. He notes JS lacks fma, which makes the quartic solver less accurate than in Rust, and that missing a cusp is a risk. Derived from R_d = R + d with a shared tangent angle: the offset arc length is L_d = L + d·dtheta wherever 1 + d·kappa > 0.
findings.use_for_engine: Offset analytic spines, never Bezier output. Validate |d| < R_min (concave side) per piece, using closed-form R_min: circle R, clothoid at its high-curvature end, log spiral b·s_min. Trim or stop lines where this fails, the d_stop idea. Offset arc length is closed form, so stations on offset lines are free. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_curve

findings.item: Euler-spiral parallels and GPU stroke expansion: Levien 2021, Levien and Uguray 2024
findings.facts: The parallel curve of an Euler spiral has curvature kappa(s) = c/sqrt(s - s0) + 1/l, with c = a/sqrt(2 l^3) and s0 = -a^2/(2l) (Wieleitner 1906), and at most one cusp per segment. The Euler-to-cubic 'parabola rule' has 5th-power error scaling. A polynomial Hermite approximation takes about 7 ns versus 240 ns for the secant method. In the 2024 paper (arXiv 2405.00127), cubics become Euler spirals with empirically fitted error estimates (mean estimate/true ratio 1.656), and halving reduces the fit error 32x. Output is an unordered line soup, not a simple polygon; evolute segments are emitted twice so nonzero winding renders correctly. Experiments use a 0.25 device-pixel tolerance. Several constants are empirical, and no code licence is stated in the text.
findings.use_for_engine: Two lessons transfer to SVG. (1) Clothoid spines make offsets and curvature combs cheap and cusp-predictable. (2) Strokes can be filled nonzero without boolean unions, if inner loops are avoided by the width < R rule or handled. The GPU line-soup pipeline itself is not needed. Blog: https://raphlinus.github.io/curves/2021/02/19/parallel-curves.html

findings.item: Logarithmic spiral: exact formulas and the golden case
findings.facts: From Wikipedia: r = a·e^(k·phi), tan(alpha) = k (alpha is the pitch), curvature = 1/(r·sqrt(1+k^2)), arc length L(phi1, phi2) = (sqrt(k^2+1)/k)(r2 - r1), and from the pole r/sin(alpha). A scaled spiral is congruent by rotation, and the spiral is congruent to its own involute, evolute and pedal. Derived and checked numerically: radius of curvature rho = k·s (s from the pole), intrinsic theta(s) = theta0 + ln(s/s0)/k, golden k = ln(phi)/(pi/2) = 0.30635, pitch 17.0324°, growth per turn phi^4 = 6.8541. Two copies rotated about the same pole never intersect: along any ray their radii differ by a fixed factor e^(-k·delta).
findings.use_for_engine: Closed-form evaluation; stations by angle or by arc length, both invertible. For Bezier output, fit one equal-angle sector once and stamp the rest by spiral similarity (scale e^(k·dphi), rotate dphi about the pole), which gives exact self-similarity. Use rotated copies about the pole for nested engraved lines around a scroll eye. Stop short of the pole and end in a G2 'eye' circle of radius k·s_eye centred at the centre of curvature.

findings.item: Log-aesthetic curves (LAC): closed-form angle functions, numeric positions
findings.facts: Per Nagy, Yoshida and Hoffmann (arXiv 2105.09762), summarising Yoshida and Saito. Standard form: the reference point is at the origin with radius of curvature 1 and tangent along +x. Radius of curvature: rho(theta) = e^(Lambda·theta) if alpha = 1, else ((alpha-1)·Lambda·theta + 1)^(1/(alpha-1)). Tangent angle versus arc length: theta(s) = (1 - e^(-Lambda s))/Lambda if alpha = 0; log(Lambda s + 1)/Lambda if alpha = 1; otherwise ((Lambda alpha s + 1)^(1 - 1/alpha) - 1)/(Lambda(alpha - 1)). Lambda = 0 gives a circle. All alpha = 1 curves are similar. Points need numerical integration. The G1 Hermite fit uses bisection. The 'drawable region' shrinks sharply for alpha < 0 or alpha > 1, which the extended LAC enlarges. G2 between segments comes from matching the first tangent length. Ziatdinov, Yoshida and Kim 2012 (CAGD 29(2)) give incomplete-gamma closed forms; I did not open that paper.
findings.use_for_engine: Implement LAC as one more intrinsic theta(s) family on the shared Gauss-Legendre evaluator. Expose alpha as a 'curve character' dial with presets: clothoid alpha = -1, golden spiral alpha = 1 with Lambda = 0.306. Special-case |alpha - 1| and |alpha| near 0. Leave LAC Hermite solving to a later phase.

findings.item: Hobby splines in JS/TS
findings.facts: jakelow hobby.js is ISC (Copyright 2020 Jake Low) and based on Jackowski's TUGboat paper. npm hobby-curve 0.2.1 (ISC, published 2022-11-04, 6.9 KB, TypeScript, no dependencies) offers createHobbyCurve(points, {tension, cyclic}) returning an SVG path, and createHobbyBezier; it credits vlad-x and Schindler ports. @thi.ng/geom-splines 2.3.95 (Apache-2.0, 'STABLE - used in production', 2026-08-25) offers cubicHobby2(points, closed, omega), cubicFromArc (an elliptic arc as 1-4 cubics) and closest-point/split helpers, but pulls in several @thi.ng packages. The earlier research (01) documents Hobby's limits: it is only approximately G2, non-local, and unstable near collinear knots.
findings.use_for_engine: A preview spline while dragging knots, and the fallback when Spiro fails. Port hobby.js (about 200 lines, ISC) rather than adding a dependency. npm: https://registry.npmjs.org/hobby-curve

findings.item: Superellipse (cartouche, jewel, rounded-panel outlines) and Knuth's construction
findings.facts: From Wikipedia: |x/a|^n + |y/b|^n = 1, parametric x = ±a·cos^(2/n)(t), y = ±b·sin^(2/n)(t) (t is not the polar angle). For n > 2 the curvature is zero at (±a, 0) and (0, ±b). For 1 < n < 2 it grows without bound at those points. Piet Hein's Sergels Torg used n = 2.5 with a/b = 6/5. Area is 4ab·Gamma(1+1/n)^2/Gamma(1+2/n). Knuth's plain.mf macro superellipse(r,t,l,b,s) joins the 4 extreme points through 4 diagonal points s[...] with directions {t-r} and so on, using bounded '...' Hobby joins. It works for 0.5 ≤ s ≤ 1. Derived: a true superellipse has superness s = 2^(-1/n) (0.7071 for a circle, 0.758 for n = 2.5). Also derived: because kappa = 0 at the vertices when n > 2, a superellipse quadrant joins a straight side with G2.
findings.use_for_engine: A 'cartouche' primitive with exponent n and aspect ratio. Build it from Knuth's 8 knots, or sample and fit with the generic fitter (it needs an arc-length table). Split it at the vertices to insert straight runs with G2 joins. Source of the macro: https://mirror.ircam.fr/pub/CTAN/systems/knuth/dist/lib/plain.mf

findings.item: Arc-length parameterisation and lookup tables
findings.facts: kurbo's cubic arclen chooses adaptively between 8, 16 and 24-point Gauss-Legendre rules using error estimates, subdividing up to depth 20. inv_arclen solves s(t) = target with the ITP method (as robust as bisection, usually faster), integrating only the increment between successive guesses. Levien's 2018 post: 9th-order Gauss-Legendre is a good compromise. Random cubics at 1e-4 needed a mean of about 3.4 subdivisions, timed at 231 ns at 1e-4 (Rust). A 24-point rule (bezier.js) undershoots on sharp kinks. Polyline flattening converges only as O(sqrt N). For the intrinsic families arc length is the parameter itself (line, arc, clothoid, LAC) or closed form (log spiral), and offsets have L + d·dtheta.
findings.use_for_engine: Only imported Beziers, superellipses, weave strands and variable-width edges need tables. Store cumulative Gauss-Legendre lengths at 32-64 nodes per piece; invert by binary search plus 1-2 Newton steps (or ITP). Animated arrows running along a track then move at constant speed with tangent alignment from the same table. Code: https://github.com/linebender/kurbo/blob/main/kurbo/src/param_curve.rs

findings.item: Sinusoidal weave strands along a curved spine: validity conditions (derived) and the current spike
findings.facts: Derivation with Frenet frame (T, n) and signed spine curvature kappa: strand centre c(s) = p(s) + w(s)·n(s) with w = A·cos(2·pi·s/lambda + psi). Then c'(s) = (1 - kappa·w)·T + w'·n, so the strand stays regular and does not fold if A < R_min of the spine on the concave side. On the inner side the wave is compressed by (1 - kappa·w). Ribbon edges are offsets of c at ±h, so they need h < the strand's radius of curvature. On a straight spine its peak curvature is A·k^2 with k = 2·pi/lambda, which gives h < lambda^2/(4·pi^2·A). With two strands in antiphase the crossing angle is 2·atan(A·k), so A = tan(crossing/2)/k. The current spike, framing/generators/weave.ts, uses exactly this cosine offset, but takes normals by finite differences (±0.5u) on sampled polylines and emits polylines.
findings.use_for_engine: Make the strand an analytic Fittable with exact c' and c'', sent through the shared fitter. Expose crossing angle, period and ribbon width as the designer's parameters, derive the amplitude, and show the A < R_min and h < lambda^2/(4·pi^2·A) checks in the lab.

findings.item: Variable-width stroke expansion: perfect-freehand and the analytic alternative
findings.facts: perfect-freehand 1.2.3 (MIT, 2026-02-01, 5.7k stars). getStroke(points, {size, thinning, smoothing, streamline, simulatePressure, easing, start/end {cap, taper, easing}}) returns outline polygon points. The README's getSvgPathFromStroke turns them into a quadratic-midpoint path. By default the outline 'include[s] self-crossings', and the README suggests polygon-clipping to flatten them. streamline and smoothing deliberately move the input path. Analytic alternative (derived): left and right edges p(s) ± w(s)·n(s), each regular while w·kappa < 1, fitted with the shared fitter and filled nonzero. Caps are an SVG arc or a taper to w = 0. Note that the normal offset differs from the true moving-circle envelope where w' ≠ 0.
findings.use_for_engine: Use the analytic edge outline for ribbons, swelling engraved lines and leaf blades: exact and deterministic. perfect-freehand at most for a 'pencil sketch' mode in the lab, never for printed output.

findings.item: G2 joins between different families: rules (Spiro and Bertolazzi-Frego sourced; the rest derived)
findings.facts: Every piece carries (theta, kappa) at both ends. G1 means theta is continuous; G2 means kappa is continuous too. Rules: (1) line ↔ arc: insert a clothoid ramping kappa 0 → 1/R (railway transition; Spiro's '[' ']' knot types do line-to-curve). (2) clothoid ↔ log spiral at station s_j: set the clothoid's end kappa to 1/(b·s_j). A clothoid can also match the spiral's kappa' = -1/(b·s_j^2), a G3 contact, because kappa1 is free. (3) log spiral ↔ circle (volute eye): circle radius = b·s_j, centred at the spiral's centre of curvature there. (4) A child sprouting tangentially from a parent at station s starts with the parent's (point, theta(s), kappa(s)), which makes it G2 at the split. (5) Fixed endpoints with G1 data need 1 clothoid (Bertolazzi-Frego); with G2 data, 3 clothoids. The existing spike framing/math/turtle.ts chains lines and arcs only, so its joins are G1 with curvature jumps.
findings.use_for_engine: Upgrade the turtle to a 'Cesàro turtle' (line, arc, clothoid, log spiral, LAC pieces), so G2 holds by construction. Close the end conditions (land on an anchor) by Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt over 1-3 free piece parameters. The lab shows a G2 check and a curvature comb at every join.

findings.item: Library landscape (npm metadata as of 2026-10-10)
findings.facts: spiro 3.0.1: Apache-2.0/MIT, 2024-04. bezier-js 6.1.4: MIT, last published 2023-07-16, repo pushed 2024-08, 77 open issues, no bundled types. paper 0.12.18: npm 'MIT', 2024-07-17, 12.3 MB unpacked. paperjs-offset 2.2.1: MIT, 2026-07. @flatten-js/core 1.6.14: MIT, 2026-08. polygon-clipping 0.15.7: MIT, 2023-12. polyclip-ts 0.16.8: MIT, 2024-12. clipper2-js 1.2.4: BSL, 2024-01. @stdlib/math-base-special-fresnel 0.3.1: Apache-2.0, 2026-02. @thi.ng/geom-splines 2.3.95: Apache-2.0, 2026-08. hobby-curve 0.2.1: ISC, 2022-11. svg-arc-to-cubic-bezier 3.2.0: ISC, 2019. cornu-spline 0.6.0: MIT OR Apache-2.0, created 2026-06-16, 0 GitHub stars, 487 KB, depends on opentype.js, unvetted. kurbo: Rust only, no official npm or WASM package found. libspiro: GPL-3.0, do not port from it.
findings.use_for_engine: Runtime dependency budget: `spiro` only, and even that is optional. Port the small algorithms with permissive licences: hobby.js, Levien's integ_spiro and fit_euler, Bertolazzi-Frego buildClothoid, and later kurbo fit.rs. Lab-only and optional: bezier-js or paper.js for SVG import and inspection, polygon-clipping for unioned hit areas.

findings.item: Numerical determinism across browsers
findings.facts: From MDN: 'Many Math functions have a precision that's implementation-dependent', and results can differ between browsers, and even for one engine on a different OS or architecture. Levien also notes that JS lacks fma, which hurts quartic-solver accuracy.
findings.use_for_engine: Do not rely on bit-identical geometry. Round SVG coordinates (2-3 decimals at local units), test against closed forms with tolerances, keep iteration counts fixed, and add root polishing (one Newton step) after closed-form polynomial solves.

findings.item: Animation along a track (later phase)
findings.facts: MDN marks CSS offset-path as Baseline 'Widely available' since March 2022, with path(), url(#svg-shape), ray() and basic shapes; examples animate offset-distance with offset-rotate: auto. I did not verify from the spec how offset-distance percentages are measured (presumably path length).
findings.use_for_engine: For the 'arrows run along their track on tab change' effect, either give the browser the fitted track path (offset-path: path(...)) or drive the position from the engine's own arc-length table in requestAnimationFrame. The JS route keeps G2-smooth tangents and exact station semantics.

gaps.recommendation:
CURVE TOOLKIT PLAN for the frame engine. Plain TypeScript, no framework, about one module per family, all behind two interfaces.

(A) `Intrinsic` describes a piece by length L and theta(s), kappa(s), and provides point(s), tangent(s), normal(s), plus endState() = {x, y, theta, kappa}. Stations are always arc length s, or u = s/L.

(B) `Fittable` provides sample(t) → {point, derivative} and cuspIn(range)?. Derived curves implement it: offsets, weave strands, width edges.

Output to SVG goes through one fitter, with tolerance in device px at the current zoom (for example 0.1 px). All geometry is solved in local units, never stretched non-uniformly.

PER FAMILY
1. Line: kappa = 0. Exact; SVG L.

2. Circular arc: kappa = 1/R, theta = theta0 + s/R, points in closed form.
   - Output an SVG A command (exact). Inside fitted outlines, use cubic arms (4/3)·tan(dtheta/4)·R with dtheta ≤ 60-90°. Measured error 2.7e-4·R at 90° and 1.8e-5·R at 57°.
   - Pitfall: arms = L/3 is 50-9000x worse.

3. Clothoid / Euler spiral: kappa = kappa0 + kappa1·s, theta = theta0 + kappa0·s + kappa1·s²/2.
   - Evaluate points by composite 16-point Gauss-Legendre over sub-pieces each turning ≤ pi/2. Measured ≤ 1.5e-8·L on one pi-turn piece and about 1e-13 on two. Cache cumulative nodes.
   - Optional fast path: port Levien's integ_spiro (order-12 Taylor, 1e-9, Apache-2.0/MIT).
   - Do not use standard Fresnel with completing the square near kappa1 ≈ 0: cancellation (Bertolazzi-Frego).
   - Builders: (a) Cesàro-turtle append, G2 by construction. (b) Two-point G1: port Bertolazzi-Frego buildClothoid (Newton with guess 20b, 3-5 iterations, BSD-2), or Levien's fit_euler (secant, ≤ 10 iterations, throws). (c) Two-point G2: 3 clothoids, later only.

4. Euler-spiral spline through designer knots (the dominant sweeps):
   - Use npm `spiro` 3.0.1 (Apache-2.0/MIT, used by Iosevka) with point types corner, g2, g4, left, right.
   - Consume spiroToArcsOnContext output and fit it yourself, or call spiroToBezier with delta ≈ 0.25 rad. The default of 1 rad leaves about 0.26% of R error.
   - Wrap every solve: check for NaN, bend > pi and end-tangent residual, because the solver returns no status after 10 iterations. Fall back to Hobby, and to the last good solution during drags.

5. Logarithmic / golden spiral: b = ln(phi)/(pi/2) = 0.30635, pitch 17.03°, phi^4 = 6.854 growth per turn.
   - Formulas: r = a·e^(b·phi); s from the pole = r·sqrt(1+b²)/b; rho = b·s; theta(s) = theta0 + ln(s/s0)/b. All closed form, no quadrature.
   - Bezier: split into equal-angle sectors (≤ 45-60°), fit the first sector once, then generate the others by spiral similarity (scale e^(b·dphi), rotate dphi about the pole). This gives exact self-similar copies and a measured 6-8 cubics per turn at 0.05-0.01u.
   - Pitfalls:
     - Stop before the pole and close with a G2 eye circle (radius b·s_eye, centred at the centre of curvature).
     - Use a circle branch when b < 1e-6.
     - An offset of a log spiral is not a log spiral. Nested lines around an eye should be rotated copies about the pole, which never cross and have geometric spacing. Use true offsets only where d < b·s_min.
   - Flame: place the tip curve's stations at equal dphi. Leaves are the same prototype scaled by r_i/r_0 and rotated with the spiral tangent. Each leaf side is a log-spiral or clothoid piece.

6. Log-aesthetic curve (LAC; generalises 3 and 5): theta(s) has a closed form per alpha branch (0, 1, otherwise), and rho(theta) is closed form.
   - Points come from the same Gauss-Legendre integrator.
   - Expose alpha as a 'curve character' dial with presets: clothoid alpha = -1, golden alpha = 1 with Lambda = 0.306.
   - Hermite solving (Yoshida/Nagy bisection; limited drawable region for alpha < 0 or alpha > 1) is phase 3.
   - Special-case alpha near 0 and near 1.

7. Hobby: port hobby.js (ISC, about 200 lines). Use it only as the live-drag preview and the Spiro fallback; it is approximately G2.

8. Superellipse (cartouche, jewel, panels): |x/a|^n + |y/b|^n = 1.
   - Build it like Knuth's plain.mf: 8 knots, with the diagonal points at superness s = 2^(-1/n) and tangents parallel to the vertex chords. Alternatively sample it and fit with the generic fitter (it needs an arc-length table).
   - For n > 2 the curvature is 0 at the vertices, so straight runs inserted there join with G2.

9. Derived curves, all `Fittable`:
   - Offset p + d·n. Curvature kappa/(1 + d·kappa); arc length L + d·dtheta. Guard |d| < R_min on the concave side, else trim or stop.
   - Weave strand p + A·cos(2·pi·s/lambda + psi)·n. Guards: A < R_min of the spine and half-width h < lambda²/(4·pi²·A). The designer sets crossing angle, period and ribbon width; the engine derives A = tan(crossing/2)·lambda/(2·pi).
   - Variable-width edges p ± w(s)·n with w·kappa < 1 and smooth w. Caps are an arc or a taper to w = 0. Fill nonzero.
   - Mirror, similarity and spiral-similarity copies, and Illustrator imports (cubic Beziers).

10. Arc length: native for families 1-6. Only imports, superellipses, strands and edges need tables: cumulative Gauss-Legendre lengths at 32-64 nodes per piece, inverted by bisection plus Newton (or ITP). The future arrow animation reads the same table.

11. Fitter.
   - Phase 1: equal-turn subdivision (≤ 30-45°), symmetric arms = chord/(3cos²(dtheta/4)), sampled maximum-distance check by projection (16-20 samples), recursive halving. Measured: 2-3 cubics for the 54° clothoid limb, 2-3 for the 170° ring, 10-13 for a 2.5-turn volute.
   - Phase 2: port kurbo fit.rs plus common.rs (area/moment quartic with Orellana-De Michele, ITP, Gauss-Legendre tables; Apache-2.0/MIT; about 1k Rust lines) for asymmetric O(n^6) fits, cusp breaks, the line fallback and the long-arm penalty. The same port simplifies imported Illustrator paths.

12. Robustness:
   - Solve in a chord-normalised frame and track unwrapped theta.
   - Cap iterations and return {value, status, residual}.
   - Fallback chain: Spiro → Hobby → last good solution, with hysteresis while dragging.
   - Lab validators: curvature comb, kappa jump at joins, d·kappa and w·kappa margins, fit error, and a golden readout (slope of rho/s).
   - Round SVG output to 2-3 decimals. Write unit tests against closed forms; for example, one golden turn ending at r = 45 must have chord 45(1 - phi^-4) = 38.4346.

SUGGESTED ORDER
1. Intrinsic pieces (line, arc, clothoid, log spiral) with the Gauss-Legendre evaluator, and the Cesàro turtle with G2 checks.
2. Phase-1 fitter and SVG emitter, then offsets and the weave strand with guards.
3. Spiro wrapper plus Hobby fallback for knot-drawn sweeps.
4. Width outlines and arc-length tables (this also enables the animation).
5. kurbo fit port, the Bertolazzi-Frego G1 connector, LAC, superellipse.

Runtime dependencies: `spiro` only, and optional. Keep the existing spike's fitRepeats; replace its polyline outputs with the fitted path.
cautions: My measured numbers (Gauss-Legendre accuracy, arc handle errors, cubic counts) come from scratch scripts in (local scratch file) (glacc.mjs, arcerr.mjs, fitexp.mjs, fitexp2.mjs, chk.mjs), not from a source. 'Best arms' used a crude grid optimiser with equal-length pieces and a sampled maximum distance. Treat the counts as order-of-magnitude, and copy the scripts into docs/research/analysis if they should be kept.

Several formulas are my own derivations, not quotes: rho = b·s for log spirals, offset arc length L + d·dtheta, the weave validity bounds A < R_min and h < lambda^2/(4·pi^2·A), the crossing-angle relation, superness s = 2^(-1/n), the G2/G3 join rules, the non-crossing of rotated log spirals, and the arm rule chord/(3cos^2(dtheta/4)). They are standard differential geometry or quick algebra, but should be unit-tested.

spiro-js returns no convergence status (10 Newton iterations, then it silently returns). Its default Bezier output (bend ≤ 1 rad, arms = derivative/3) is visibly inaccurate at this drawing's scale, about 0.2u on the ring. Levien himself documents Spiro's non-unique solutions, wild loops and loop reversal at cusps.

Licences: libspiro is GPL-3.0, so do not port from it. Port from raphlinus/spiro or spline-research (Apache-2.0/MIT since the 2019 relicensing) or use spiro-js. The Clothoids library is BSD-2-Clause. The Levien-Uguray paper text states no code licence. Cephes code in stdlib is Apache-2.0 with Moshier's notice.

Standard Fresnel evaluation of clothoids via completing the square loses precision as kappa1 → 0 (near-circles and near-lines), which is common in the medallion limbs. Use Gauss-Legendre quadrature or the Taylor integrator, or small-parameter series as in Bertolazzi-Frego.
Log spirals blow up in curvature at the pole. Never evaluate down to s = 0; end in an eye circle. Uniform Gauss-Legendre pieces converge slowly near the pole, so use the closed form.

Offsets of log spirals and clothoids are not the same family. Offsets of Beziers are degree-10 curves. Any offset or width larger than the local radius of curvature makes cusps and loops: guard it, do not hope.

kurbo's fit error is an approximation to the Fréchet distance, and its docs say it is 'not a rigorous guarantee'. Levien-Uguray's error constants are empirical. Fitting is still 'work in progress' by the author's own account. There is no official npm or WASM kurbo, so a TS port is real work (about 1k lines of Rust including the quartic solver). JS lacks fma, so expect slightly less accurate quartic roots than in Rust and add Newton polishing.
G2 Hermite data (fixed points, tangents and curvatures at both ends) cannot always be met by one or two clothoids; three are needed (Bertolazzi-Frego 2018). Don't promise a single-piece G2 connector.

LAC Hermite solving has limited 'drawable regions' for alpha < 0 or alpha > 1 and needs branch handling near alpha = 0 and alpha = 1. Keep it out of the first phases. I did not open Ziatdinov et al. 2012 (incomplete-gamma forms); the speed-up claims for it from secondary sources disagree (10x vs 13x).
MDN says JS Math function precision is implementation-dependent, so geometry will not be bit-identical across browsers. Round output and test with tolerances.

perfect-freehand outlines self-cross and its streamline/smoothing options move the input path, so it is unsuitable for exact printed linework. cornu-spline (npm, created June 2026, 0 stars) is unvetted. bezier-js was last published in July 2023, and its offsets are reliable only on 'simple' segments.

Not verified: the minimax circle constants on Mortensen's page (the numbers were not extractable as text), and how CSS offset-distance percentages are measured (MDN page excerpt did not say). Iosevka's final outline step (solving Spiro through the offset knots) was inferred from spiro-expand.mjs and not traced into spiro-to-outline.mjs.

catalog.overview:
CURVE CATALOG: "the right curve for the job". This is grounded in docs/research/01-07 and the curve-math gap research. Items marked (derived) are my own algebra, checked numerically in scratchpad/catalog_check.mjs. Items marked (uncertain) need testing in the Lab.

SEVEN RULES BEHIND EVERY ENTRY
1. Define every curve intrinsically: length L, tangent angle theta(s) and curvature kappa(s) over its own arc length.
   - Arc length then comes free, so stations, ticks, beads and motion all use s or u = s/L.
   - A G1/G2 join becomes a comparison of (x, y, theta, kappa) at both ends.
   - Closed forms cover the line, arc and log spiral. Clothoids and log-aesthetic curves (LAC) use composite 16-point Gauss-Legendre (GL); no Fresnel functions are needed (curve-math research).
2. Choose the family by curvature profile, not by look-alike shape.
   - 01-curve-systems.md principles: curvature should be monotone between knots, peak at the knots, and stay G2 across joins.
   - 03-golden-growth.md #5 (Hubner): people prefer the true golden spiral over the quarter-circle Fibonacci spiral, mainly because its curvature is continuous.
   - So curvature jumps are the main thing that separates "printed" from "hand-assembled".
3. Use the measured drawing (07-drawing-analysis.md) to pick each family.
   - Medallion S-limbs are clothoids (R2 0.98; kappa grows as s^1.10, lower limb as s^1.58).
   - The ring is a circle (r 85.76, RMS 0.54).
   - Flame tips lie on a log spiral (free b 0.488; golden b forced gives RMS 0.39).
   - The volute #103 is a tight log or Archimedean spiral (b 0.14-0.16, 2.5-2.8x growth per turn).
   - Leaves, crest hearts and ring loops are exact similarity copies. The crest and side leaf are mirrors.
   - Fans converge on circle anchors with roughly even spacing.
4. One family covers almost everything (derived). When curvature grows as a power of distance from an inflection, kappa ∝ sigma^p, the curve is a log-aesthetic curve with alpha = -1/p.
   - The upper limb (p 1.10) is alpha -0.91, effectively a clothoid (alpha -1). The lower limb (p 1.58) is alpha -0.63.
   - The log spiral is alpha +1.
   - So a single "curve character" dial covers sweeps, stems, curls and leaves, with clothoid and golden-spiral presets (01 #4, 03 #8).
5. "Golden" means phi applied by construction where a curve is self-similar, never hunted for in drawings (07 caution: any ratio is within 12% of some half-power of phi).
   - Sharp's menu (03 #4) gives phi per Theta: b = ln(phi)/Theta.
     - Theta = 54 deg: b 0.5106, pitch 27.05 deg, 24.7x per turn.
     - 90 deg: b 0.3063, 17.03 deg, 6.854x.
     - 108 deg: b 0.2553, 4.97x.
     - 144 deg: b 0.1915, 3.33x.
     - 180 deg: b 0.1532, 8.71 deg, 2.618x.
   - Two useful matches (derived; a 6-item menu, so treat them as design options, not discoveries):
     - phi per 54 deg (pentagon) sits in the flame-tip RMS minimum (b 0.50 gives RMS 0.21). It keeps the drawn character and is still phi-derived.
     - phi per 180 deg (b 0.153, 2.618 per turn) falls inside the measured #103 volute range (b 0.144-0.16, 2.47-2.76 per turn).
   - phi also sets radii and ratios (ring/medallion = phi^k, stem gaps, crossing pitch). It never sets fan spacing: 07 shows uniform spacing, and phi spacing collapses the inner lines.
6. Copies, not re-solves. Use similarity copies (gnomon, 03 #1), mirrors and rotations for repeats. This gives exact self-similarity, and the Bezier output is fitted once and stamped with transforms.
7. Re-solve at every size; never stretch non-uniformly (01 §2.7: an affinely scaled circle is an ellipse). Responsive change works through parameters:
   - Continuous parameters interpolate.
   - Discrete ones (counts, topology, family choice) switch at room thresholds with hysteresis, and the switch cross-fades (thresholds research).

OUTPUT
All geometry goes through one fitter at a tolerance in device px.
- Exact circles are emitted as SVG A.
- Fitted cubics use arc-corrected arms, chord/(3cos^2(dtheta/4)), on equal-turn pieces. Measured counts:
  - 2-3 cubics for the 54-degree limb or the 170-degree ring.
  - 6-8 per golden turn.
  - 10-13 for a 2.5-turn volute, at 0.05-0.01u.
- Never use L/3 arms on bends over about 0.25 rad: they are 50-9000x worse.

OTHER STYLES
They mostly need straight segments, arcs and offsets, so the same kernel serves them.
- Three-centred and circular arches keep exact concentric offsets, so archivolt profiles stay exact. Elliptical arches do not.
- A G2 corner (clothoid easement or superellipse with n > 2) is the modern-card and moulding counterpart of the ribbon easement.
- Ticks, beads, rays and chevrons are punctuation placed at fitted stations.

UNCERTAIN, TEST BEFORE RELYING ON IT
- The lower-limb alpha (R2 0.93).
- The guilloche "touch" waveform formula (mine).
- The squircle-to-circle size calibration.
- CSS corner-shape support.
- Live offset-path:url() updates.
- All cubic counts (crude optimiser, order of magnitude).

entries.job: Medallion S-sweeps and stems (dominant curves of the corner)
entries.family: Clothoid (Euler-spiral) pieces chained in a Cesaro turtle: straight stem -> clothoid limb (kappa 0 -> 1/R_ring) -> circular ring arc -> clothoid limb. A limb can be generalised to a log-aesthetic limb with a 'character' exponent p (alpha = -1/p). Knot-drawn variants use a Spiro (Euler-spiral spline) through on-curve knots.
entries.why:
Measured in 07-drawing-analysis.md Q2a.
- Upper limb of #113: 135u long, turning 51-54 deg, curvature growing from 0 to 0.0139. Clothoid R2 0.980; power law k~s^1.10 R2 0.988; log spiral R2 0.03. Forcing a golden spiral costs RMS 1.31 and max 3.16u and looks wrong.
- Lower limb: k~s^1.58 (R2 0.93) against clothoid 0.80. Parallel #114 behaves the same (p 1.16 and 1.48).
A clothoid's curvature ramps linearly from the inflection, the 'one clean ramp' that 01-curve-systems.md calls fair: monotone between knots and G2 at joins. That is why the sweep reads as engraved rather than drawn. Derived: kappa ∝ sigma^p measured from an inflection is exactly an LAC with alpha = -1/p (-0.91 upper, -0.63 lower), so one dial reproduces both limbs. Levien's Spiro (01 #3) is the knot-based authoring form of the same family. Stems are straight (07: stem x positions 32.94/44.45/61.34/72.85).
entries.math:
Clothoid piece: kappa(s) = kappa0 + kappa1·s, theta(s) = theta0 + kappa0·s + kappa1·s^2/2. Points are x(s) = x0 + ∫cos theta, y(s) = y0 + ∫sin theta, by composite 16-point Gauss-Legendre on sub-pieces turning ≤ pi/2 (measured 1.4e-9·L for a pi turn on one piece, 7.5e-14 on two). A limb from the inflection (kappa 0) to the ring (1/R) turns kappa_end·L/2, which checks against the drawing: 0.0139·135/2 = 53.8 deg.
Power-law limb (LAC alpha = -1/p): kappa(sigma) = kappa_end·(sigma/L)^p and theta(sigma) = theta_i + kappa_end·L/(p+1)·(sigma/L)^(p+1). It turns kappa_end·L/(p+1), with p = 1 being the clothoid. The inflection is a sign change of kappa through 0 inside one curvature program (02 #3, Xu and Mould), never two arcs butted together.
Closing: the far end must land on an anchor (a ring station, or the exit at the ring's E point where #114 ends). Solve by Newton/LM over 1-3 free piece lengths, with the status and residual returned.
Golden by construction, applied to radii only: R_ring = R_medallion·phi^k. Drawn 1.20; k = 0.5 gives 1.272 (+5u). Stem middle/outer gap = phi (drawn 1.467, +1.7u).
entries.designer_parameters:
- sweepTurn: total turning of each limb, 30-120 deg (drawn about 54).
- character p: 1.0-1.8. 1 is clothoid; the drawn upper limb is 1.1, the lower 1.6.
- ringStep k: R_ring = R_med·phi^k, k 0-1, preset 0.5, or free 'as drawn 1.20'.
- exitAnchor: named station on the ring, e.g. E = 0 deg, or an angle.
- stemLength: not a slider. It comes from the layout and stretches.
- stemGapRatio: middle/outer gap, 1.3-1.8, preset phi.
entries.joins:
- Stem line to limb: G2 for free, since the limb starts at kappa = 0.
- Limb to ring: G2, with the limb's end kappa set to 1/R_ring.
- Ring to second limb: G2.
- The sweep is a ROOT of the attachment graph. It inherits only from the corner box and the medallion circle; everything else (fans, loops, leaves, weave sockets) inherits its tangent and curvature at stations on it.
- Spiro knot types: corner, g2, left/right for line-to-curve.
entries.implementation:
Arc length is native (s is the parameter), and the ring is closed form.
- Bezier, phase 1: equal-turn split to ≤ 30-45 deg, symmetric arms = chord/(3cos^2(dtheta/4)), sampled max-distance check by projection (16-20 samples), recursive halving. Measured 2-3 cubics per limb at 0.05-0.01u.
- Bezier, phase 2: kurbo fit.rs port (area/moment quartic, O(n^6)).
- Parallel sweeps such as #114 and double engraved lines are true offsets of the analytic spine: p + d·n, kappa_d = kappa/(1 + d·kappa), L_d = L + d·dtheta (closed form, so stations on the offset are free). Guard |d| < R_min on the concave side.
- Swelling lines are filled outlines p ± w(s)·n with w·kappa < 1, filled nonzero.
entries.pitfalls:
- spiro-js returns no convergence status (10 Newton iterations, silent). Wrap every solve: NaN, bend > pi or end-tangent residual triggers the fallback chain Hobby -> last good solution.
- Do not use spiro's default Bezier output (1 rad pieces, L/3 arms): about 0.2u error on the ring.
- No Fresnel completing-the-square near kappa1 ≈ 0 (near-lines and near-circles lose precision; Bertolazzi-Frego).
- Never stretch the medallion. When its slot shrinks below the room threshold, swap the variant (medallion -> simple block) rather than squash it.
- The lower-limb alpha comes from an R2 0.93 fit: medium confidence.
- Spiro blows up when knots move far (06 caution), so drag handles should edit 1-2 parameters, not raw knots.

entries.job: Medallion ring (circle, its bands, loops and anchor stations)
entries.family: Exact circle, concentric offsets for bands, and rotation copies for ring loops. Not an ellipse: the drawn ellipse is rx/ry 1.039, an intended circle.
entries.why:
07 Q2a/Q4 measurements:
- The ring arc (170 deg) has curvature CV of only 0.18 and fits a circle at r 85.76, RMS 0.54.
- The medallion ellipse is 72.78 x 70.06.
- Anchors sit at named points: tendrils at the leftmost point, fan B at about 52 deg below E, #114 at the rightmost point, and loops #40-48 ending on the circle.
- Ring loops are near-copies at a mean 28 deg step (CV about 10%).
